#5173. Horizen Holders Face November 4 Bridge Cutoff Before L3 Wind-Down

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Horizen users have a near-term operational deadline as the project winds down its layer-three network. Its official migration notice sets November 4 at 13:00 UTC as the bridge cutoff and directs holders to review the instructions for their particular assets.

The migration plan includes a later recovery process for certain remaining balances. That is not a universal guarantee for every token or wallet arrangement, making the difference between an ordinary withdrawal and a delayed recovery especially important.

A chain shutdown is different from a token being removed from an exchange. In the exchange case, the underlying network may continue to function normally. A network wind-down changes the infrastructure through which users can submit instructions and applications can update state.

That makes the location of an asset consequential. A token bearing the same name can exist in more than one environment, and the procedure for moving it depends on where the balance is actually recorded. A holder should not infer their position from a ticker in a portfolio tracker alone.

There is also a timing distinction between initiating an exit and receiving its result. Bridging can involve stages that finish after the first transaction. A successful submission is useful evidence, but the recipient-side balance and the bridge’s own status determine whether the transfer has completed.

Horizen says its later DAO return covers ZEN and qualifying ETH balances, while USDC.e is outside that process. The notice also flags special handling for smart-contract wallets and a minimum ETH balance threshold. Readers with affected holdings need the current official instructions rather than a generic assumption that all balances will be returned automatically.

These distinctions reflect an important feature of blockchain accounting: recognizing an address on two networks does not establish that the same kind of account exists on both. A simple wallet and a contract-controlled account can require different treatment when balances are reconstructed elsewhere.

Similarly, a bridged asset may be operated through infrastructure with obligations separate from those of the chain’s own project. A recovery programme can only make reliable promises about assets and processes within its stated scope.

The project attributes the accelerated transition to compatibility issues connected to Base’s Denim upgrade. Base’s published specification introduces a different block cadence and associated data changes, illustrating why infrastructure built on another chain must track its dependencies.

A layered system can borrow useful components and reduce development work. It can also inherit assumptions about how the underlying network behaves. When those assumptions change, the dependent service may need a migration rather than a routine version update.

This is a broader architectural lesson rather than evidence that all layer-three networks face the same outcome. The relevant question is which exact dependencies a system has and whether its operators can adapt them before an upstream change takes effect.

Moving activity to an established network can simplify the number of places where an ecosystem must maintain infrastructure. For users, however, the immediate benefit depends on successful balance transfers, working applications and clear communication about what happens to existing positions.

A staking interface being unavailable, for example, would not by itself establish that funds have disappeared. Equally, a roadmap promising future staking would not prove that a particular balance has already migrated. Transaction records and official recovery notices answer those different questions.

The November 4 cutoff is therefore the central fact for this week. The broader move to Base can be evaluated over time, but the asset-specific exit and recovery instructions deserve attention before the operating environment changes.

Leading Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange and Ripple blockchain payments partner Mercado Bitcoin has announced a temporary freeze on cryptocurrency deposits and withdrawals after acknowledging a security breach.

As the firm revealed in an official announcement, the security breach did not cause any harm to its users or compromise their personal data.

“We detected and quickly mitigated a security issue in one of our systems this morning,” Mercado Bitcoin said.

Mercado Bitcoin stressed that the incident did not harm any customers or lead to a data breach.

Nevertheless, as a precautionary measure, the firm decided to temporarily halt deposits and withdrawals while its security teams conduct further investigations into the issue and try to locate any assets that could have been affected.

Additionally, Mercado Bitcoin said that it is working with the appropriate authorities to investigate the incident.

In the latest update, Mercado Bitcoin revealed that it continues to work on restoring its operations to normal.

“We are still working to safely restore operations and will keep our customers updated on our official channels,” the exchange announced.

Interestingly, the company also released some cryptocurrency wallet addresses related to suspicious transactions linked to the incident.

The move aims to assist blockchain investigators and other industry players in keeping track of possibly compromised assets on different networks.

According to preliminary analysis shared by blockchain security firm Hypernative, the incident allegedly involved more than $40 million in suspicious cryptocurrency transactions across various blockchain networks.

The list includes Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), Tron (TRX), Polygon, Arbitrum, Avalanche, BNB Smart Chain and Stellar (XLM).

Meanwhile, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino revealed that more than 4.5 million USDT tied to the security incident were frozen by the stablecoin issuer.

Mercado Bitcoin is known for having a strong partnership with San Francisco-based blockchain firm Ripple.

#5171. Crypto Hack Losses Hit $8.74 in 2026, More Than Triple 2025, Yet Without Binance the Year Ran Quieter: How Did Bitcoin and Ethereum React After Major Hacks?

Crypto hack losses hit $8.74B in 2026 vs $2.51B in 2025. Here’s how Bitcoin and Ether moved a day, a week and a month after major hacks.

Crypto hack losses reached $8.74 billion in 2026 by October 31, more than three times the $2.51 billion lost over the same ten months of 2025, after the October 29 Binance breach alone added $6.36 billion.

Take Binance out and the picture flips. The rest of 2026 comes to $2.38 billion, about 5% less than 2025 at the same point, even though attackers hit 325 targets against 120 a year earlier. More attacks, smaller hauls, and then one enormous one.

The market has its own pattern. Across the ten largest hacks since January 2025, Bitcoin’s move on the day of the attack ranged from -4.1% to +1.9%. A month later, for the nine with a full month of data, the range ran from -15.5% to +19.9%, and it followed whatever the broader market was doing.

The 2025 hacks landed in falling markets, and every one was followed by a lower Bitcoin price a month later. Most of 2026’s landed in rising ones.

So how bad has 2026 really been, and what does history say about the weeks after Binance?

The size of the biggest theft. Through September, 2026 was running behind 2025: $2.24 billion lost against $2.48 billion. Then Binance lost $6.36 billion across ten blockchains in one night, more than all of 2025’s hacks put together.

The two years share a culprit. The FBI tied 2025’s largest crypto hack, the $1.4 billion Bybit theft on February 21, to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and Chainalysis now ties Binance to the same unit. The biggest hacks of each year:

The rest of 2026 looks different from 2025 too. There were 325 incidents through October, almost three times 2025’s 120, and five 2026 hacks topped $290 million, against one in 2025. Stolen keys and cross-chain bridges did most of the damage outside Binance.

The gross number also overstates what stays lost. CertiK’s October tally counts $3.03 billion frozen or returned, mostly Binance funds caught on-chain, which cuts the month’s adjusted losses to about $3.47 billion. Trackers also disagree on the year: CertiK puts 2026 at $9.2 billion gross and 2025 at $3.35 billion, while DefiLlama has $8.74 billion and $2.72 billion.

DISCOVER: Binance Hacker Sits on $1.4 Billion in Bitcoin, Triple a Week of ETF Buying

A small dip on the day, then the market’s own trend. The heatmap compares Bitcoin and Ether with their close the day before each of the ten biggest hacks since 2025.

Bybit is the closest match to Binance: a North Korean exchange theft over $1 billion. Bitcoin lost 14.2% within a week of it, with US tariff fears weighing on markets that week too, and it was still 12.4% lower a month on.

Binance is following a gentler path so far. From the October 28 close to Monday:

Neither yet. Bitcoin trades at $77,870 on Binance, flat on the day, and has held above its October 30 low of $76,326 for three days, right on the 200-day EMA (exponential moving average) at $76,512.

After Bybit, Bitcoin lost its floor within a week. After most of 2026’s hacks, it was higher a month later. The line between the two is clear on the chart: the 200-day EMA below, and the 50-day EMA at $80,293 above.

The crypto hack record says the first day rarely decides much. What Bitcoin does at the 200-day EMA over the next few weeks will show which path this one takes.

#5169. Devcon Opens in Mumbai This Week With Ethereum Builders Facing a Delivery Test

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

For people following Ethereum from the market side, the useful task is to separate ideas presented on a stage from changes that developers can actually test and users can eventually rely on. A conference creates a concentrated view of the work; it does not turn every proposal into a network commitment.

A protocol idea can be persuasive before its operational consequences are fully understood. It may improve one property, such as transaction handling, while adding costs elsewhere, such as data storage or the difficulty of running infrastructure.

The most informative technical presentations explain those trade-offs and offer a way for others to inspect the work. A specification, reproducible benchmark or test implementation gives outside developers something they can challenge. A performance target without those materials is harder to evaluate.

There is also a sequence between research, agreement on scope, client implementation, testing and activation. A talk about one stage should not be reported as completion of the next. This matters especially when short clips circulate without the qualifications that accompanied a presentation.

The Ethereum Foundation’s original Mumbai announcement described a gathering extending beyond protocol engineering. That wider participation matters because improvements in the underlying network only reach users through products, interfaces and operating processes.

A wallet team, for example, might need to turn a complex authorization into something a person can understand before signing. A payments developer needs to handle delayed confirmations and mistaken inputs. An institutional application needs to reconcile its blockchain records with the obligations in its legal agreements.

These are less dramatic achievements than a headline about speed, but they can determine whether an application is dependable. A credible demonstration should show what happens when the happy path breaks, including what a user sees and how the system recovers.

Open-source ecosystems distribute responsibility across people who do not all work for the same organization. A change can require cooperation among client teams, infrastructure operators, wallet developers and application maintainers, each with different constraints.

Bringing those groups together can shorten the distance between a proposed improvement and a clear understanding of its consequences. It can also expose disagreements that were easy to miss in a written thread. A resolved incompatibility may be a more useful outcome than another product announcement.

That kind of progress is difficult to measure through attendance figures. It becomes visible later, when documentation improves, implementations converge or a previously blocked integration starts working. The follow-up work is where a conference’s technical value is ultimately demonstrated.

Useful evidence will include published materials, specific engineering milestones and clearly identified owners for the next stage of a project. Readers should be able to distinguish a proposal seeking discussion from software ready for production.

For applications, the stronger indicators are working integrations and repeated use, alongside a credible explanation of costs and failure handling. A polished demonstration can establish that an idea is possible without proving that it works reliably at scale.

Devcon’s immediate importance is bringing Ethereum’s many development efforts into view at the same time. The longer-term story will depend on what survives scrutiny and becomes usable software. Neither the schedule nor a keynote provides a dependable forecast for ETH’s price.

#5168. XRP’s Security Fix Puts Validator Trust Under Scrutiny

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP’s Security Fix Puts Validator Trust Under Scrutiny

An XRP Ledger security patch released before full code disclosure has sparked debate over vulnerability management and validator influence.

A security patch released before its full code was made public is at the center of a dispute over XRP Ledger governance. In a video addressing the controversy, Kamilah Stevenson, a finance commentator and longtime XRP holder, argues that the restricted disclosure protected the network rather than substantiated allegations of fraud.

The criticism came from Cyber Capital fund manager Justin Bonds, who, according to Stevenson, challenged both the upgrade process and the influence of recommended validator lists. The dispute raises two distinct questions for investors: how developers handle dangerous vulnerabilities, and how much discretion network operators retain.

Stevenson says a researcher reported an overflow vulnerability through the XRP Ledger’s bug bounty program on September 22. The flaw, which she says had existed since around 2015, potentially allowed an attacker to obtain XRP improperly or create unauthorized tokens.

According to her account, developers released version 3.4.1 on September 25 without immediately publishing the full fix code. More than 80% of main validators upgraded that day, and an amendment activated on October 9, leaving nodes without the update unable to remain synchronized.

Dr. Stevenson reports that a subsequent ledger audit found no exploitation or unauthorized XRP creation. The transcript does not identify the auditor or provide the underlying report.

She compares the response with Bitcoin Core’s handling of a 2018 vulnerability: developers initially disclosed a crash risk, withholding its inflation implications until users had time to upgrade.

“You protect the network first and you explain second,” she says. That comparison supports delayed vulnerability disclosure, though it does not by itself resolve concerns about inspecting the XRP update.

Stevenson acknowledges that publishers of recommended Unique Node Lists wield influence because many operators adopt those defaults. Operators can choose their own lists, she says, while Ripple runs only one validator on the most commonly used list.

She also points to the amendment threshold: more than 80% validator support sustained for two weeks. Those safeguards challenge the idea that Ripple can unilaterally rewrite ledger rules, but validator ownership alone does not settle questions about influence over defaults.

In a nutshell, the promised code release and technical write-up would offer firmer grounds for judging this episode than either a fraud allegation or assurances from an XRP holder.

The end of October 2026 was marked by the largest incident in the history of the crypto market — the $6.3 billion hack of the Binance exchange. This case exposed the vulnerability of the instant exchange (swaps) infrastructure.

While the automated systems of the North Korean group TraderTraitor withdrew $242 million via the Tron blockchain in the first two days, decentralized bridges and liquidity aggregators de facto became the main tool for legalizing the stolen funds.

Against this backdrop, the head of NEAR Intents Alex Shevchenko issued a warning to cryptocurrency wallet developers. His position is pragmatic: focusing exclusively on finding the best rate for the user turns services into unwitting accomplices in cybercrimes.

Since around $3.5 billion still remains under the hackers’ control after a wave of emergency freezes, regulatory pressure on the Web3 sector will inevitably increase. To minimize risks, the head of NEAR Intents formulated three basic survival rules for modern crypto wallets when choosing integration partners:

For wallet developers, the problem is structural. A single swap often passes through several protocols at once — an aggregator, a bridge and multiple liquidity pools — and each hop dilutes responsibility.

If any link in this chain processes tainted funds, the wallet through which the transaction was initiated shares the reputational damage and, increasingly, the legal exposure.

This is why due diligence on integration partners is shifting from an optional step to a core product requirement.

Investments in compliance and integration security are no longer a boring formality. The market has reached a point where the reputational and legal cleanliness of a service is valued far higher than saving a few cents on fees.

#5165. Solmate Discloses 1.26M SOL Custody Positions and Says It Has No Binance Exposure

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Solmate Infrastructure has published a specific answer to a question facing crypto treasury companies after an exchange security incident: where are the assets held? In an October 30 disclosure, the company said it had no Binance accounts or exposure and identified the custodians holding its reported 1.26 million SOL.

The Form 6-K places those holdings with Kraken, Anchorage Digital or BitGo as of October 29. It is a company statement about custody at a particular time, rather than an independent audit of every position.

A corporate balance sheet can show exposure to a cryptocurrency without explaining the complete operating arrangement behind it. Investors also need to know who controls transactions, how transfers are approved and whether the company can access the assets when it needs them.

A treasury that plans to hold for years still faces shorter-term obligations. It may need cash for operating costs, collateral for financing or flexibility to respond to an unexpected event. Custody arrangements influence how quickly it can meet those needs.

Publishing the names of service providers improves the starting point for that analysis. It does not reveal the allocation among them, every account condition or the extent to which assets may be committed to another activity. Those details require additional disclosures.

During a security event, markets can struggle to distinguish companies directly affected from those sharing only a connection to the same asset class. A precise statement can reduce that uncertainty without making broader claims about the safety of the industry.

Solmate’s accompanying release says its validator infrastructure continued to operate normally. That addresses another part of the business: the systems participating in network operations, as distinct from where the treasury tokens are held.

The distinction is useful because an operating interruption and a custody loss are not interchangeable. A company could experience one without the other. Reporting them separately makes it easier to understand what an incident has actually changed.

Using more than one custodian can reduce dependence on a single operating platform, but it also creates work. A company must reconcile several records, maintain consistent authorization rules and understand the conditions for moving assets between accounts.

A simple example is a treasury policy requiring two approvals for a transfer. That rule must be enforceable wherever assets are held, rather than exist only in an internal document. Differences among service providers can become important when staff change or an urgent transfer is requested.

There is no evidence in this disclosure of a weakness in Solmate’s procedures. The point is that naming several providers is one component of risk management, not a complete description of it. Clear allocation and operational reporting would give shareholders a fuller view.

The number of SOL held is different from the cash value available to shareholders. That value changes with the token’s price and with the company’s wider liabilities, operating costs and financing structure.

A statement that assets are accounted for therefore cannot be translated into a guarantee about equity value. Nor does an unchanged custody position establish that tokens can be sold at a particular price without affecting execution.

Solmate’s filing is useful because it answers a bounded question with named counterparties and a dated balance. Investors assessing the company can combine that information with subsequent financial reports and operating disclosures, keeping asset safekeeping, liquidity and market exposure as separate parts of the analysis.

#5164. Lisk Officially Shuts Down Blockchain After 10 Years

Long-standing blockchain project Lisk has officially ended its blockchain operations after 10 years of existence, moving on to a new financial platform for businesses.

Lisk announced on Nov. 2 the official shutdown of its blockchain after 10 years of existence. This marks the end of one of the longest-lived blockchains in the crypto world.

"Today, the Lisk Chain has officially shut down," the project said in an X post.

With the blockchain shutdown, Lisk has ended its Portal and Bridge services. The rest of the blockchain's infrastructure is also being powered down.

The blockchain shutdown marks a significant milestone in the evolution of the Lisk project, which was launched in 2016 and has seen several changes over the years.

The Lisk team, however, has noted that the shutdown of the blockchain does not spell the end of the Lisk project.

The company is transforming into a new financial platform, one that enables businesses to manage both traditional currencies and stablecoins in one place.

"For 10 years, Lisk built onchain with developers, stakers and holders that made Lisk what it is," Lisk said.

The Lisk project has made it clear that its native token, LSK, will continue to exist even as the blockchain closes shop.

According to the team, LSK will still exist on Ethereum as the loyalty token for its new business financial platform.

In addition, the project announced plans to burn approximately 5.23 million LSK tokens left in its staking rewards pool.

The total figure includes unallocated rewards to users as well as unclaimed earned rewards.

The LSK tokens are set to be burned, permanently removing them from circulation. This will also lower the overall supply of the cryptocurrency.

This comes after a large burn of LSK tokens in September. At the time, Lisk burned 100 million LSK tokens after making the decision to wind down its decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) through a governance vote.

The burn event reduced the LSK token's supply from 400 million to 300 million LSK.

Lisk intends to introduce new use cases for LSK in 2027. This will allow businesses to earn rewards in the token and use LSK for platform fees.

#5163. Hashdex Adds Jane Street to Crypto Index ETF Authorized Participants

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Hashdex Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF has added Jane Street Capital to its list of authorized participants, according to an October 30 prospectus supplement. The document updates the firms able to participate in the product’s creation-and-redemption arrangements.

It is a market-structure development rather than a statement that Jane Street has made a long-term investment in the fund. That distinction matters when institutional names become attached to crypto products.

The SEC’s investor glossary describes authorized participants as financial institutions that enter contractual arrangements to buy and redeem creation units. Their role links the supply of a fund’s shares to activity in the market where those shares trade.

Most ordinary investors transact with another market participant through a brokerage account. An authorized participant operates at a different layer, dealing with larger blocks under the product’s documented procedures. The two activities support the same product but should not be confused.

A listed participant can make the infrastructure available without committing to create shares on every trading day. The appointment establishes a relationship and a permitted function. Actual activity depends on market conditions, commercial decisions and the rules governing the fund.

When demand for shares changes, the mechanisms for adjusting supply can influence how closely the traded price stays connected to underlying asset value. If those mechanisms are difficult or expensive to use, gaps can persist even when traders recognize them.

An additional participant may offer another route through which the market can respond. That can be useful if existing firms face their own balance-sheet constraints or operational interruptions. It does not guarantee narrower spreads, because execution also depends on the liquidity of the assets and the cost of hedging.

Consider a period when investors want to buy shares rapidly while underlying crypto markets are moving. A firm providing liquidity has to manage the price risk between the share transaction and the corresponding asset trade. Access to a creation process is necessary for some workflows, but it does not make that exposure disappear.

The Hashdex supplement also identifies an affiliation between Jane Street Capital and a crypto trading counterparty. Such disclosures help readers understand how firms involved in different parts of the process are connected.

The relevant analytical question is whether the structure can process orders reliably and on competitive terms. An institutional service relationship is not evidence that the firm expects the underlying cryptocurrencies to rise or that it will retain a directional position.

This is particularly important when reading fund-flow headlines. Net new shares, secondary-market turnover and an authorized-participant appointment describe different things. One concerns changes in product size, another concerns trading between holders, and the third concerns the operating network behind the product.

Useful follow-up measures include trading spreads, premiums or discounts and the consistency of creation and redemption activity. Those observations would show whether the expanded network changes the experience for investors.

They also need context. A wider spread during an unusually volatile session does not automatically establish that the fund’s structure has failed. Comparing conditions over time and against underlying-market liquidity is more informative than judging a single quote.

The October filing is a relatively small document with a meaningful operational purpose: it updates who can help connect the fund to its underlying markets. It adds a recognizable financial firm to that machinery, while leaving the investment case and future flow direction open to separate assessment.

#5158. WalletConnect Adds Stellar Payments as Bermuda Ticketing Rollout Targets 2027

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

WalletConnect is expanding payment access on Stellar while preparing a separate merchant rollout in Bermuda. Its October 29 announcement says WalletConnect Pay supports the network, with LOBSTR as the first live Stellar wallet.

The Bermuda initiative, developed with Penrose Partners, begins with ticketing platform Premier Tickets, or PTIX. That integration is expected in the second quarter of 2027, so wallet support available now should be distinguished from the planned merchant launch.

A payment interface needs to identify both the customer’s wallet and the transaction the merchant expects. Those tasks sound simple until an order expires, a customer changes devices or a transfer arrives after the checkout page has been closed.

For ticketing, the sequence is particularly important. The buyer wants confirmation that a seat has been secured; the organizer needs confidence that payment belongs to the correct order. A blockchain transaction hash does not, by itself, contain every detail of that commercial relationship.

A useful integration must connect payment status to inventory and customer support. Otherwise, a fast transfer can still create a slow service experience when the ticketing system cannot confidently match the money to the purchase.

The proposed PTIX arrangement sends customer funds to the event organizer’s wallet without the ticketing platform holding them. That design changes where money sits between the moment a customer pays and the moment the organizer can use it.

It can reduce the need for the platform to collect and subsequently distribute balances. It also requires careful handling of refunds, disputed orders and changes to an event. Those obligations do not disappear because the transfer takes a more direct route.

A cancelled concert offers a straightforward example. Returning a payment requires identifying the right recipient, confirming the amount and deciding which party is responsible for making the transfer. A well-designed service should make that process comprehensible to a customer who has no interest in the underlying network.

For an organizer, receiving a digital asset is useful only if it fits the business’s finances. The organizer needs to know how much usable value it has received, what costs apply and how the balance will pay suppliers or other expenses.

Some businesses may want to retain a token; others may prefer conversion into bank money. Those choices affect reconciliation and liquidity planning. The availability of a wallet connection does not establish that every merchant will make the same decision.

Payment records also need to remain useful after the event. A business must be able to connect sales, refunds and settlement to its own accounts. The more the system can handle these ordinary tasks predictably, the less specialist knowledge a merchant needs to accept the payment method.

The announced timeline gives observers a clear milestone: a functioning ticket purchase from a supported wallet, with a merchant receiving the expected funds and a buyer receiving the correct ticket. That is a more useful measure than the theoretical reach of a wallet network.

After launch, repeat use and the rate of failed or abandoned payments would help assess whether the option solves a real customer problem. Lower processing costs would matter if they survive the full journey, including conversion and support.

WalletConnect’s Stellar expansion opens a technical route, while the Bermuda project attempts to give that route a regular commercial purpose. The two developments fit together, but their different launch stages need to remain clear as the integration progresses.

#5157. TRON became an early route for stolen Binance funds, Elliptic finds

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

TRON served as a major early route for moving assets stolen in the Binance hack, according to a November 2 investigation by Elliptic. The blockchain analytics firm traced funds spreading across roughly 7,700 TRON addresses before much of the activity shifted elsewhere.

Elliptic’s summary showed how the attackers moved on some of its assets during and after stablecoin issuers such as Tether froze billions of dollars. Elliptic estimated that about $3.24 billion in digital assets were still sitting at the addresses associated with the theft at around 07:00 UTC on November 2.

Binance reported approximately $6.3 billion stolen in the October 29 attack. The FBI subsequently attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group.

According to Elliptic’s investigation, the attackers swapped 234 million stolen USDT for TRX on SunSwap before Tether froze the remaining USDT on TRON.

A distribution wallet began breaking TRX into smaller chunk transfers on October 30. The funds travelled through thousands of different addresses and crossover bridges/services that exchange assets. ​

In total, $147M was seen leaving the TRON network, almost all of which left and reached the Ethereum network as ETH.

A total time of 51 hours was used, and a total of 1,113 transfers occurred from the time the distributing wallet came into service to its last transfer. The last transfer took place on 1 November at 05:33 UTC.

In another November 1 thread, analyst SomaXBT calculated that about $242 million was laundered in roughly two days using TRON-linked routes.

Over two-thirds of the amount was allocated to routes leaving TRON (194M versus 194M). An added $22M was an estimated amount of fees, trading costs, and price change.

In both investigations, the money was moved through several services, ending up in newly created wallets, adding another layer of extra steps investigators had to follow.

By early November 1, TRON activity had largely stopped, Elliptic said. Movement subsequently picked up on Ethereum, Solana, and other networks.

Early on November 2, all 233 million stolen XRP moved to six new addresses. Elliptic also identified about 28 BTC passing through transactions that combine multiple users’ Bitcoin, complicating tracing.

Only a tiny amount was likely cashed out, according to Elliptic, meaning it is still possible for exchanges and brokers to intercept because investigators will be following the assets.

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Airtm and BVNK have announced an integration intended to let users spend wallet funds with participating retailers, extending digital-dollar services beyond receiving and holding money. The October 29 joint announcement links Airtm Connect with BVNK’s stablecoin-payment infrastructure and says the integration will use Stellar.

The commercial objective is straightforward: a balance becomes more useful if its owner can spend it without repeatedly moving through disconnected services. Delivering that convenience requires the entire payment process to work, including the steps outside the blockchain.

A customer who receives digital dollars may still need to pay merchants using a different system. Each conversion or transfer can introduce a fee, a delay and another opportunity to select the wrong details.

Connecting a wallet directly to a merchant payment flow could remove some of that handling. The user would begin with the balance they already possess, rather than first preparing money in a separate account solely for the purchase.

The improvement depends on whether the customer can understand the final cost before confirming. A low network fee is only one element. Exchange rates, payment-provider charges and any conversion into the merchant’s chosen settlement currency also determine what the purchase actually costs.

A payment option is difficult to use regularly if adding money to the wallet is unreliable. Conversely, convenient funding has limited value if the customer cannot use the resulting balance where they shop.

The partnership combines providers working at different parts of that chain. The implication is a chance to make funding, wallet access and merchant acceptance feel like one service, even when multiple organizations perform the underlying work.

Consider someone paid by an overseas customer who then purchases a subscription. A coherent flow should preserve enough information to show the incoming payment, the available balance, the purchase and any refund. If the customer must reconstruct those records across several interfaces, some of the convenience has been lost.

A successful network transaction and a completed retail order are related, but they are not identical. The merchant needs to know that the transfer corresponds to a valid order and meets its settlement requirements before delivering the product.

That creates several possible intermediate states. A customer may approve a payment after the original quote expires. A merchant may cancel an order while a transfer is processing. A service may need to reverse the commercial transaction even though the blockchain transfer itself cannot simply be deleted.

These are normal payment-system problems rather than reasons to dismiss the model. The quality of an integration shows in how consistently it handles them, especially for users who cannot afford to wait through a lengthy support process to recover a modest balance.

The announcement establishes a planned route to participating retailers. It does not imply that every merchant connected to a broader financial network will immediately accept an Airtm wallet payment.

Practical evidence would include which countries and merchants are enabled, the available funding methods and the time between payment approval and a usable settlement balance. Successful repeat purchases would say more about adoption than the number of people who could theoretically access the service.

For stablecoin markets, this is a useful test of whether digital-dollar infrastructure can support ordinary spending without adding complexity for the customer. Airtm and BVNK have described the connection they want to build. Its value will come from how well funding, checkout and after-sales support fit together once people use it.

Less than 48 hours remain before the U.S. midterm elections.

This is the first big election to follow the 2024 presidential elections that sent the crypto market into a frenzy after pro-crypto Donald Trump won.

But now that the odds of a Democratic sweep of the midterms are over 73%, it brings up the question whether crypto will do the same if the Republicans fall short.

The stakes are higher for Ripple. As the chart below shows, XRP had the most explosive rally of the post-election period in 2024. It rose over 280% in November. The key takeaway? November has historically been XRP’s strongest month, with average returns above 80%.

That naturally puts Ripple [XRP] under the spotlight ahead of the upcoming elections.

Interestingly, XRPL is exhibiting a balanced picture on-chain, as the number of transactions is currently hovering around 3.29 million, while the volume of transactions is sitting at just under $2.32 billion. Active addresses are also an important metric to monitor. While transactions are being processed, the adoption of users needs to increase.

In essence, Ripple has been relatively quiet on-chain. This raises a key question: Can XRP’s ongoing supply squeeze provide enough bullish pressure to fuel a breakout, even as on-chain demand remains subdued?

Ripple kicked off November with its scheduled 1 billion XRP escrow unlock.

However, shortly after, 700 million were re-locked, meaning that the net amount being released is actually 300 million. It’s common for a large amount of tokens to be locked back into escrow each month. In the past year, Ripple has unlocked 12 billion XRP but has also locked 8.4 billion.

This means that the real amount of supply coming into the market is far smaller than the 1 billion figure.

As can be seen in the post below, Ripple has placed 700 million XRP back in escrow through three transactions. Simply put, this means that these tokens cannot be released into the market immediately.

After the 1 billion XRP was unlocked, there are now just 300 million XRP available outside of escrow. This means less supply pressure.

Against this backdrop, XRP’s on-chain signals start to matter.

According to SoSoValue, ETFs have so far seen an impressive increase of $4.32 million in weekly inflows, surpassing last week’s $4.25 million, with the best weekly inflows since mid-September.

Combined with recent whale activity, the fact that XRP has been able to stay above $1.20 suggests it could be in an early accumulation phase.

With the midterm elections approaching, this setup puts XRP on the watchlist for a potential post-election rally, provided broader market sentiment turns bullish.

#5154. Taurus Adds Stellar Smart-Contract Assets to Institutional Custody and Issuance

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Taurus has expanded its Stellar integration to support smart-contract-based assets, giving institutional clients a broader set of custody and issuance functions. The company said on October 29 that the capabilities are live through Taurus-PROTECT and Taurus-CAPITAL.

The official announcement describes an extension of existing Stellar support rather than a newly announced fund or security. The change matters because institutions need more than a place to store a token once it has been created.

Safekeeping is often described as protecting private keys. For an institution, a useful custody system must also govern what those keys are allowed to authorize, who can request an action and which approvals are needed before it proceeds.

A simple transfer and a smart-contract interaction can carry different consequences. An instruction may change an allowance, invoke a contract function or alter how an asset can be handled. The approving person needs enough information to understand that consequence before a signature is produced.

This creates a practical reason to integrate smart-contract support into the tools an institution already uses. A separate experimental interface may be technically capable of sending an instruction while sitting outside the organization’s normal operating controls.

Creating a tokenized instrument requires decisions about the rights it represents and the actions permitted after issuance. Depending on the instrument, those may include transfers, subscriptions, redemptions or changes governed by the issuer’s rules.

Taurus says the release supports several Stellar token models, including structures intended for regulated assets. That flexibility can help an institution match its technical implementation to the instrument it wants to offer, rather than treating every token as economically identical.

It also raises an integration question: can the legal and operational records remain consistent with the contract state? A token should not appear transferable in an application when the issuer’s rules prohibit the intended recipient from holding it.

A financial firm considering another blockchain faces costs beyond deploying a contract. Staff need familiar approval processes, finance teams need reports and operations teams need a procedure for handling failed instructions.

Reusing an established custody and issuance interface may reduce the number of new systems those teams must learn. It can also make oversight more consistent across networks, provided the interface still exposes the differences that matter.

For example, an operations dashboard should not imply that two assets have identical settlement behaviour simply because they appear in neighbouring rows. Network-specific requirements, contract permissions and servicing obligations need to remain visible where they affect decisions.

The release establishes that clients have more infrastructure options on Stellar. The next evidence of adoption would be institutions using those capabilities for named instruments with clearly explained ownership and transfer arrangements.

There is a difference between supporting a contract standard and completing a reliable asset-servicing process. A production service must handle routine transactions, unusual requests and the reconciliation that follows. Its value lies in reducing the effort required to do those jobs correctly.

For Stellar, the potential benefit is a wider route for institutional asset activity. For Taurus clients, it is the ability to consider another network without rebuilding every surrounding control. Neither outcome should be measured simply by the number of token standards listed in a release.

The more revealing test is whether an issuer can take an asset from creation through ongoing management and eventual redemption using a coherent set of records. Taurus’s announcement expands the available toolkit for that work; actual products and operating results will show how effectively it is used.

#5153. Bitcoin slides below $77,000, BNB drops amid Binance hack

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

BNB lost 7.1%, while Binance Co-CEO Yi He pledged that the exchange will cover all user losses resulting from the hack.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $77,000 late Thursday, alongside declines in other major cryptocurrencies, as the Binance exploit intensified a market-wide sell-off.

The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped 4.5% over the past 24 hours to trade at $76,664 as of 10:00 p.m. ET Thursday, according to The Block's bitcoin price page.

BNB (BNB), the native cryptocurrency that powers the Binance ecosystem, lost 7.1% to change hands at $698.65. Ethereum slid 5.2% to $2,190, while XRP fell 7% to $1.21.

Crypto liquidations totaled $1.55 billion over the past 24 hours, with 246,482 traders liquidated, according to CoinGlass data. Those included $1.34 billion in long positions. The largest observed liquidation order was on Binance-BTCUSDT, valued at $11.09 million.

The crypto market decline coincided with a major Thursday hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that roughly $5.9 billion was stolen at the time of the theft.

"The Binance exploit has intensified market-wide selling, with BNB facing the greatest exposure. About $1.5 billion in 24-hour liquidations, predominantly long positions, has amplified pressure on BTC and ETH," Dominick John, analyst of Zeus Research, told The Block.

"Market recovery hinges on Binance restoring confidence in exchange security and customer funds," John added.

However, Rick Maeda, head of Markets at Laevitas, suggested that the market reaction to the Binance hack appears to be "fairly contained" and that the BNB's drop was "quite modest for possibly the largest exchange theft ever."

"The exchange's $144 billion assets under custody, the fact that they paid a $4.3 billion penalty to the U.S. government in 2024 for AML breaches with no issue, as well as the swift responses from stablecoin providers such as Tether and Circle to freeze over $2.4 billion have all contributed to the lack of panic across the industry," said Maeda.

Jeff Ko, chief analyst of ViaBTC, shared similar views. "I don't expect the stolen BTC to add much selling pressure," said Ko. "The broader crypto market was already leaning bearish, which is why the sell-off spread so quickly across the board. That said, I believe Binance can absorb the loss comfortably."

Binance said on X that the currently verified frozen amount from the hack is around $3 billion. Binance Co-CEO Yi He also said that the exchange will cover all user losses resulting from the hack.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said Coinbase is "doing everything we can to support in the current situation," including blocking transfers to compromised wallets.

"Moments like this call for the industry to work together," Armstrong added.

#5151. Trezor reports suspected hardware implant in Safe 5 sold by CryptoBilis

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Trezor has not received the device but is treating the risk as credible, urging customers who used units sold by CryptoBilis since March 2026 to move their funds.

Trezor urged customers who purchased hardware wallets from reseller CryptoBilis since March 2026 to migrate their funds immediately, following a responsible disclosure alleging a physical hardware implant in a Safe 5 device.

The Czech hardware wallet maker removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network earlier this month following reports of tampered Ledger devices sold through the same distributor.

In a blog post published Friday, Trezor said it received the disclosure on Oct. 28 regarding a unit bought in August 2026 through Tokopedia. The company has not received the device for in-depth examination but it interviewed the customer by video call and is treating the report as credible, it added.

"We'd rather warn people now than wait for confirmation and find out someone lost their funds in the meantime," Trezor CCO Danny Sanders said in a statement to The Block. "If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, move your funds to a new wallet and contact our Support team, and we'll send you a new device."

According to the post, the reported implant consists of an additional circuit board fitted between the device's main board and screen. It contains a cellular module and antenna that can reportedly read information displayed on the screen, including a wallet's recovery phrase, and transmit it over a mobile network.

Trezor said it began inspecting devices purchased from the reseller after removing it from its network. The company has received four customer devices for examination so far and said it found no signs of tampering in those units.

Rival wallet maker Ledger previously confirmed physical tampering in signers sold through CryptoBilis, while OneKey similarly severed ties with the reseller, froze new approvals, and offered free replacements.

For Trezor's part, no user funds loss has been reported. Onchain analysts estimated losses tied to the Ledger incident at more than $86 million across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tron, but the wallet maker has not confirmed those figures.

Meanwhile, the CryptoBilis incident is not the first security headache for Trezor this year. In August, a breach at shipping provider ShipMonk exposed personal data belonging to about 13,700 customers.

In September, Trezor disclosed that another approximately 67,000 U.S. customers were affected by the same breach. Also in the same month, the company said a breach at its third-party email provider had enabled phishing messages to be sent from Trezor's official domain.

#5150. Core Lightning nodes can keep crashing after an upgrade until a stored trigger is removed

The flaw was patched in April, but a malicious announcement already saved on an affected node needs separate removal.

A disclosed flaw in Core Lightning, software for Bitcoin’s Lightning payment network, can leave a node crashing on restart even after an upgrade because the malicious announcement that triggered it remains on disk.

Researcher Nishant Bansal’s October 24 disclosure identifies versions v25.02 through v26.04 as affected. Once the announcement is saved, restarting reloads the same trigger. Bansal says the operator must manually remove the offending record to restore the node.

Bitcoin Optech highlighted the issue on October 30, but the preventive patch is months old. Core Lightning merged PR #9082 on April 24 and shipped the fix in v26.04.1 on April 25. The October disclosure explains a flaw whose preventive fix had been available since April.

Channel announcements tell nodes about connections in the Lightning routing graph. In this case, an announcement named the same previously unknown node as both endpoints. Vulnerable software accepted it and wrote it to its on-disk gossip_store before loading it into the routing graph.

The graph then tried to insert that node twice. A safeguard against duplicates aborted gossipd, the component handling these announcements, and Core Lightning treated that failure as fatal to the whole node.

The patch checks the endpoint ordering before accepting an announcement. Requiring the first node ID to be strictly less than the second also rejects equal IDs. This stops the malformed input from being accepted and stored.

The new validation check applies to incoming announcements. Startup still reads records already in gossip_store, and upgrading does not remove the malicious record saved before the crash.

Bansal’s recovery requirement is manual removal of the malicious record from gossip_store. Cleanup alone also leaves a vulnerable installation open to another crash: the disclosure says an attacker can resend the same announcement while the attacker-controlled funding output remains unspent.

Bitcoin Optech notes that Core Lightning releases before v25.02 could accept and relay such announcements without crashing themselves. An attacker therefore did not need a direct connection to every vulnerable node.

For operators choosing an upgrade now, v26.04.1 marks the first fix for this defect. As of November 2, the project’s latest release is v26.06.9, issued October 7, which maintainers strongly recommend installing.

Downtime carries a payment-monitoring risk beyond unavailable service. Bansal warns that an offline node cannot watch the chain for a revoked channel state or a time-limited payment claim that must be made before expiry. Missing those events can put funds at risk.

#5149. Coinbase Q3 net income jumps 66% as prediction markets gain traction

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Bernstein analysts said Coinbase's expanding prediction markets and derivatives businesses helped offset weaker spot trading activity.

Coinbase Coinbase Global, Inc. (COIN) reported a sharp jump in third-quarter net income to $719 million, as its expanding prediction markets and derivatives businesses helped offset weaker spot trading activity, analysts said.

According to the exchange's earnings report released Thursday, the company generated $1.22 billion in total revenue, broadly flat from the previous quarter but down 35% year over year.

The company's net income rose 66% year on year to $719 million from $433 million in the same period last year. The results included a $715 million gain on crypto assets held for investment, compared with a $424 million gain in the year-ago quarter.

The exchange's spot trading volume fell 8% quarter over quarter to $135 billion, though the platform continued to gain market share, according to the report.

Notably, Coinbase's prediction markets business surpassed $200 million in annualized revenue, doubling from roughly $100 million in the previous quarter.

"Prediction markets have been one of the fastest-growing products in Coinbase history, growing even through slower sports months driven by crypto contracts where we have a strong right to win," Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said in a Thursday statement.

Bernstein analysts wrote in a Friday research note that the growth in prediction markets and subscription and services revenue "helped offset the softer crypto trading activity."

The analysts estimated that prediction markets and derivatives accounted for about 25% of the company's transaction revenue, equivalent to roughly 12% of its total revenue.

Coinbase's derivatives trading volume declined 7% quarter on quarter to roughly $986 billion, while the industry derivatives volumes declined by 11% quarter on quarter, according to Bernstein.

"Subscription and services revenue grew quarter over quarter and now represents nearly half of net revenue. Prediction markets are adding another revenue stream and are less correlated to crypto volatility," said Coinbase CFO Alesia Haas. "These businesses make Coinbase more diversified and resilient across market cycles."

Meanwhile, stablecoin-related revenue remained a key contributor to Coinbase's results. Its stablecoin revenue came in at $328 million, up 3% quarter on quarter. That figure included $21 million attributable to USDC held in corporate balances.

William Blair analysts said Thursday that stablecoins, particularly USDC, will revolutionize cross-border payments and "play a critical role in tokenized RWA settlement."

Both Bernstein and William Blair reiterated their Outperform ratings on Coinbase following the earnings release. Bernstein maintained its $250 price target on Coinbase's stock, while William Blair's valuation analysis suggested the stock could be worth roughly $240.

Coinbase's Nasdaq-listed shares closed down 1.07% at $160.59 on Thursday.

#5147. ETH vaults lagged staking while dollar strategies beat Treasuries, Glassnode finds

Glassnode’s September review found ETH vaults lagged staking while dollar strategies beat Treasuries for a third month.

ETH vaults in Glassnode’s September comparison trailed staking even as the balance in its wider vault sample rose about 15% to $10 billion. Curators managing dollar-denominated vault strategies beat Treasuries for a third consecutive month, according to the research firm’s October 30 performance review.

Vaults pool deposits into yield strategies overseen by curators, or managers. The split puts a practical question ahead of the advertised yield: what could the depositor have earned while keeping the asset they already wanted to own? For an ETH holder, earning more tokens through a managed strategy is useful only in relation to alternatives such as staking. A dollar saver faces a different comparison.

Glassnode’s balance figure, its highest since November 2025, describes the vaults represented in its data. It does not establish whole-market growth or isolate how much came from new deposits, changing asset values or changes in coverage. A growing pool of assets and a strategy that beats its benchmark are separate findings.

A depositor who intends to retain ETH exposure is choosing how to put that holding to work. Comparing an ETH vault with staking preserves that starting decision. Comparing it with a dollar interest rate also introduces a decision about whether to hold ETH at all.

CryptoSlate’s October 24 staking analysis made that distinction between accumulating tokens on an existing holding and shopping for cash income. Glassnode’s new September comparison brings the question inside managed DeFi: did the additional strategy deliver more than staking?

The ETH vaults in Glassnode’s comparison did not clear staking’s return hurdle. That makes the relevant test the return above staking, after allowing for the vault’s additional risks.

The dollar result carries a different implication. Beating Treasuries shows a return premium against that comparator, but says nothing on its own about whether the premium adequately paid for the vault’s additional risks. The next question is what generated the income and what could interrupt access to the money.

The yield-data provider vaults.fyi’s benchmark explainer separates USD and ETH yields by network. Its current methodology weights up to five of the largest qualifying vaults by their total value locked, with a $1 million minimum for each. Its legacy Ethereum mainnet ETH benchmark instead uses four fixed liquid-staking tokens.

The construction matters: those series cannot be assumed to be Glassnode’s staking comparator. Currency and return dates must match before any return gap can be measured.

The accounting is particularly consequential for strategies built on liquid-staking assets. Part of the total return can come from the underlying staking position and part from what the vault does with it. Treating the strategy’s extra yield as the entire ETH return can understate performance; adding staking again to an inclusive total can overstate it.

Vaults.fyi’s APY methodology distinguishes fully compounded total yield, including underlying protocol yield, from intrinsic yield earned by the underlying asset alone. Its March product update described that separation as a way to distinguish the asset’s earnings from the strategy’s contribution.

The same discipline applies to costs. Vaults.fyi derives trailing annualized yields from onchain share-price changes and accounts for fees already reflected in share prices or accrual. Subtracting those fees again would understate the reported return. Separately valued reward-token emissions can add to the total, so the base return and incentives also need to be distinguished.

Even that split can require looking beneath a wrapper. In its separate census using data as of August 20, vaults.fyi identified cases where wrapper-level base yield contained downstream rewards. An apparently incentive-free return at the first layer can therefore still depend on incentives further along the allocation chain.

Later yield tables cannot settle the September comparison. Vaults.fyi’s October 26 ETH snapshot listed Lido stETH at a 2.34% seven-day average APY. That is an annualized rate from a later trailing window, not September’s realized staking return or a matched test of Glassnode’s vault cohort.

Morpho’s October 8 ecosystem report said more than $11 billion sat in curated vaults. That broader category is separate from Glassnode’s tracked sample.

For individual depositors, the contract and allocation matter more than a platform total. Morpho’s Vault V2 documentation describes adapters that route funds into underlying strategies and caps that can constrain collateral, oracle or protocol exposures. The enabled adapters, actual allocations and configured limits determine which exposures a user takes.

V2 permits performance fees up to 50% of yield and management fees up to 5% of assets, while distribution wrappers can add another fee layer. Those are configuration ceilings, not actual charges for Glassnode’s sample. The V2 framework illustrates why the version, fee schedule and allocation of each chosen vault matter.

Exit rights add another dimension. Morpho V2’s in-kind mechanisms can exchange vault exposure for an underlying protocol position that may still be illiquid. A penalty of up to 2% may apply, and optional gates can restrict withdrawal rights. Leaving a vault is therefore not always the same as receiving immediately spendable ETH or dollars.

Staking, the ETH comparator, has constraints too. Liquid-staking protocol Lido’s withdrawal process uses a first-in, first-out queue, with waits depending on available ETH, queue demand and validator exits. Users remain exposed to slashing while queued. Selling stETH on a secondary market provides another route, but the execution price can differ from ETH.

That makes the September split a starting point for judging managed DeFi. Dollar curators cleared their reported Treasury hurdle while the ETH vault comparison failed to clear staking’s. For a depositor, the remaining test is whether the return above the relevant alternative survives the actual fee and incentive accounting and compensates for the specific collateral, contract and exit risks taken to earn it.

#5145. Coinbase (COIN) Misses Revenue Estimates as Users Fall, Armstrong Sets Up New Share Sales

Coinbase missed revenue expectations as users declined, despite growth in recurring revenue, while executive share-sale plans and a massive Binance security breach added pressure to crypto markets.

Coinbase had a mixed third quarter. Revenue came in at $1.20 billion, below the $1.233 billion analysts expected, according to company filings. Subscription and services revenue did better, reaching $570 million. The company is still heavily tied to trading activity, but its recurring income is growing.

Monthly Transacting Users fell to 7.4 million, down from 9.3 million a year earlier. During its earnings call, Coinbase blamed overall market conditions. Its share of crypto trading volume did rise to 10.7%, the fourth straight quarter of gains, which suggests it is winning business even as the broader market quiets.

JUST IN: Coinbase disclosed buying 643 Bitcoin worth $1.5 billion for its balance sheet in Q3 🚀 pic.twitter.com/5BYdrwLCJN

Separately, filings reported on October 30 show CEO Brian Armstrong has set up a plan to sell up to 8.17 million Class A shares. He adopted the plan in August under SEC Rule 10b5-1, which lets executives schedule sales ahead of time. Sales could run from November 16 through October 2027, subject to stock price conditions. Co-founder Fred Ehrsam and President Emilie Choi have similar plans, bringing the total to about 13.6 million shares.

This is not new territory for Armstrong. In the past, VanEck analyst Matthew Sigel tracked about $545.7 million in sales over nine months, starting in April 2025. Armstrong has said these sales are part of his risk management, not a signal about the company.

Coinbase shares (COIN) fell about 15% today, but not necessarily due to this earnings report.

Binance disclosed a security breach on October 29 that it estimates at $6.3 billion, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Around $3 billion in assets has been frozen so far, with industry partners assisting in the freezes.

The hackers are allegedly linked to North Korea, though Binance has not attributed the attack to any group. The exchange says it has found no evidence of a leaked wallet private key.

Binance says it has $6.34 billion in reserves available to cover losses. Deposits were unaffected, and the company expects to resume withdrawals within 48 hours. Figures remain preliminary, and estimates vary slightly across outlets.

The market reacted quickly. Bitcoin fell roughly 4.5% to below $77,000. Shares of Strategy (MSTR) fell nearly 10% on the day. Strive (ASST) shares fell over 12% at times. Coinbase’s stock is down over 55% on the year.

#5144. Binance says it has $6.34 billion ready to cover hack losses

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Binance already holds $5 billion in affected tokens and is buying the remainder, while industry partners have frozen approximately $3 billion.

Binance has allocated $6.34 billion in its own funds and reserves to cover losses stemming from an earlier security breach, the exchange said in a statement on Friday.

The exchange was hacked on Thursday, with investigations and recovery efforts alongside law enforcement ongoing. It pegged the loss at $6.3 billion.

According to the statement, Binance is holding about $5 billion of the committed funds in the same digital assets that were affected. The exchange did not specify the tokens, but Blockaid, while flagging the incident earlier, said that it was investigating billions in outflows from Binance hot wallets across Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Avalanche.

The exchange is buying the remaining roughly $1.3 billion in tokens through market and over-the-counter channels. However, it cautioned that the process could take longer because of thin liquidity and settlement delays.

Meanwhile, the reserve does not include approximately $3 billion in assets that Binance says industry partners have frozen. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino separately said the stablecoin giant froze over $1.57 billion in USDT, while Circle confirmed more than $800 million in USDC had been frozen.

Ripple "promptly" froze roughly $200 million in associated funds, co-CEO Yi He said. World Liberty Financial also worked with BitGo and other partners to freeze approximately $27 million in stablecoins and $2 million in its own tokens, according to an X post.

In an earlier statement on Friday, Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave an attacker access to a service container used to submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

Teng noted that the incident involved a more complex process than simply exploiting one employee's permissions. Binance has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak.

"Your money is safe, and we're covering every loss," Teng wrote.

The exchange has also suspended withdrawals, but users can still deposit assets, the co-CEO said.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs said several elements of the attack resemble previous incidents linked to North Korean hackers, including last year's $1.5 billion Bybit breach. Binance has not attributed the incident to a particular group.

TD Cowen said the breach exposed risks in exchange custody and cybersecurity, but did not undermine the underlying utility of digital assets or blockchain networks.

#5142. Eclair tightens Bitcoin funding rules after unconfirmed inputs put Lightning payments at risk

The October 27 release requires confirmed peer inputs for splices by default and improves recovery when a channel must close with funding still pending.

Bitcoin Lightning developer ACINQ has urged node operators to upgrade after fixing security weaknesses that malicious peers could exploit.

The company released Eclair version 0.14.6 on Oct. 27, introducing stricter transaction requirements and recovery mechanisms to prevent manipulated channel funding from jeopardizing pending payments.

“We highly recommend upgrading, as some of these issues can be exploited by malicious nodes,” ACINQ said in its release announcement.

The warning centers on a weakness in how Lightning channels handle funding changes before the underlying Bitcoin transactions are confirmed.

Lightning allows users to transfer Bitcoin through payment channels without recording every transaction on the blockchain. Operators can also add or withdraw liquidity from existing channels through a process known as splicing.

However, ACINQ's release documentation warns that accepting unconfirmed funding inputs from another node creates an opportunity for manipulation.

A malicious peer could double-spend an unconfirmed transaction after signing a splice, invalidating the funding arrangement that supports the channel.

If the affected channel subsequently closes through Bitcoin's blockchain, pending payments secured by conditional contracts known as HTLCs could become vulnerable because their settlement depends on the invalidated funding transaction.

The developers described a potential security exposure rather than a confirmed theft, leaving the extent of any real-world exploitation unknown.

The update introduces a new security setting that requires confirmed inputs from peers before they can contribute funds to channel splices.

Enabled by default, the protection also prevents operators from building additional splices on top of unconfirmed funding changes, reducing opportunities for malicious peers to undermine settlement.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

ACINQ separated this requirement from its existing dual-funding protections, which now apply specifically to channel creation.

The developers also strengthened the software's response when a channel must close while a funding transaction remains unconfirmed.

Under the revised settlement logic, Eclair selects a commitment transaction backed by funding that its Bitcoin Core backend recognizes, reverting to the latest confirmed funding state when necessary.

That change addresses a problem in which an operator could attempt to settle a channel using a funding transaction that had disappeared from its local pool of pending Bitcoin transactions.

A related correction tackles another potential loss scenario involving transactions that miners confirm after Eclair has stopped tracking them as its preferred settlement route.

Previously, the software could misidentify such a transaction as belonging to the counterparty, potentially failing to claim funds and pending payment outputs that remained recoverable.

The new logic recognizes those transactions and attempts to recover the corresponding outputs, protecting funds that might otherwise be left unclaimed.

ACINQ also warned operators against using its optional zero-fee commitment feature when splicing with untrusted peers. That feature was already disabled by default.

The release credits security researcher Erick Cestari with responsibly disclosing issues addressed by the update.

Operators running older Eclair versions have been advised to install the patch and retain the new confirmed-input safeguard. ACINQ said existing payment channels can remain open during the upgrade, which requires stopping the software, installing the new version, and restarting the node.

#5141. Strategy’s preferred-stock fix sets up renewed bitcoin buying, analysts say

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

MSTR fell after third-quarter results, but StoneX and TD Cowen kept buy ratings, citing a $4.83 billion cash reserve and a steadier STRC preferred.

Strategy (MSTR) fell nearly 10% on Friday following its third-quarter earnings, but Wall Street remains bullish on the leading bitcoin treasury company.

Analysts say Strategy has successfully strengthened its balance sheet and stabilized its preferred-stock financing structure, although the effort came at the expense of near-term bitcoin-per-share growth.

Strategy ended the third quarter with $5.07 billion in dollar assets, including a $4.83 billion cash reserve that covers roughly 3.2 to 3.4 years of preferred dividends and debt interest, according to analyst reports from StoneX and TD Cowen.

The company also spent roughly $2 billion repurchasing its STRC preferred stock, helping restore the shares to near their $100 par value and demonstrating greater resilience in its digital credit financing model. However, Strategy's bitcoin per share declined 3.7% year to date as the company prioritized building cash reserves and supporting its preferred securities over accumulating bitcoin.

Separately, shareholders of Strategy's STRC, STRF, STRK and STRD preferred shares approved a change this week allowing dividends to accrue daily, effective Nov. 1 for STRC and Jan. 1 for the other securities.

"Management said the change was intended to reduce volatility, improve liquidity, broaden demand, and move the instruments in the direction of the tokenized, around-the-clock market that they are anticipating," StoneX analyst Mark Palmer wrote.

﻿Expand Chart

With its preferred-stock financing structure more stable and liquidity substantially improved, analysts believe Strategy is better positioned to resume bitcoin accumulation and grow its bitcoin per share.

"We view these developments as important primarily because deeper distribution and better liquidity could ultimately increase Strategy’s capacity to issue Digital Credit efficiently," TD Cowen analysts wrote. "That, rather than STRC's trading price in isolation, remains the connection to MSTR common-equity holders."

StoneX reiterated its buy rating and $435 price target on MSTR, while TD Cowen maintained its buy rating with a $260 price target.

MSTR traded down 8.7% to $129.90 per share on Friday morning. The stock is down approximately 27% year to date.

#5139. BNB’s $99 million ETF inflows came almost entirely before Binance’s hack

An early-October allocation drove BNB’s monthly ETF lead, leaving November to show how investors responded to Binance’s breach.

BNB exchange-traded funds (ETFs) led October inflows among US-listed spot crypto ETFs tracked by SoSoValue, with the largest allocation arriving weeks before Binance suffered a record $6.3 billion cryptocurrency hack.

The US-listed VanEck BNB ETF attracted $99 million during the month, ahead of $35 million for NEAR and $19 million for XRP, according to SoSoValue data.

The gains contrasted with broader withdrawals that saw investors pull $1.61 billion from Ethereum funds, $515 million from Bitcoin products and $144 million from Solana ETFs.

VanEck's BNB ETF, trading under the ticker VBNB, accounted for the category's October inflows. SoSoValue's daily flow table records about $97 million on Oct. 2, or 98.8% of the monthly net total, weeks before the attack.

The same table shows fund assets of about $3 million on Oct. 1, $100 million on Oct. 2 and $103 million on Oct. 5. Subsequent flows were comparatively small: about $1 million entered on Oct. 9 and $285,000 left on Oct. 15. BNB's strong monthly ranking came from that early allocation.

VanEck introduced VBNB on May 28 to give US investors exposure to BNB through an exchange-traded product. The fund holds the token in custody arrangements separate from Binance, using qualified custodians including Anchorage Digital and BitGo. Its shares represent exposure to BNB and not an ownership interest in the exchange.

That distinction became especially relevant after Binance disclosed that attackers compromised its hot wallets at around 20:05 UTC on Oct. 29, stealing an estimated $6.3 billion in tokens.

The exchange said it would absorb the loss using corporate funds and its Secure Asset Fund for Users, while working with issuers and investigators to freeze stolen assets.

Binance said approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. By Nov. 1, it reported having replenished about 95% of the assets affected by the theft, with purchases of harder-to-source tokens still underway.

The exchange also began reopening withdrawals in phases on Nov. 1. It said the initial surge in withdrawals had since eased.

Despite its strong monthly inflows, VBNB's assets declined from $98 million on Oct. 29 to $92 million on Oct. 30. Those figures also reflect changes in BNB's market price, meaning the decline cannot automatically be attributed to ETF redemptions.
