The last trading day of October produced a markedly different outcome in Bitcoin funds.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost roughly $643 million on Oct. 30, reversing a positive month-to-date balance and leaving October with $515 million in net withdrawals. The funds had previously been on course for a third consecutive month of inflows.

The reversal followed four consecutive sessions of Bitcoin ETF buying. Bitcoin-focused research firm Ecoinometrics, which had already warned that those inflows were too small to establish lasting demand, said the sudden selling exposed the market's vulnerability to another shock.

“ETF investors aren't buying the dip. They're selling it,” the research firm said, adding that the first serious disruption had undone October's tentative recovery.

Bitcoin had fallen below $80,000 after the Binance breach. The selloff came against a backdrop of weak ETF demand even before the incident, making it difficult to attribute every redemption solely to the hack.

Ethereum faced a deeper and more persistent retreat. Its $1.61 billion in monthly ETF withdrawals was the largest since US spot Ether funds began trading in July 2024.

The first full trading week of November will better test BNB fund demand after the breach. In a Nov. 2 update, Binance said the full zero-knowledge proof for its Oct. 31 reserve snapshot had been completed for the ten covered tokens. It said about 95% of the impacted amount had been replenished, with acquisitions of the remaining assets continuing. The exchange plans a broader snapshot on Nov. 4, followed by a proof it estimates will take 40 to 50 hours to generate.

#5136. Treasury holds $1 trillion as Bitcoin faces a key liquidity test this week

Treasury’s November financing decisions will test whether a possible cash drawdown can ease funding conditions while debt issuance competes for cash.

Treasury’s financing decisions this week will test whether a possible year-end cash drawdown can ease Bitcoin’s funding backdrop. The government held about $1,016 billion at the Federal Reserve on Oct. 28, inside the range it had anticipated for late October.

The potential relief depends on the cash assumptions Treasury updates in its Nov. 2 borrowing estimates and the issuance and buyback plans due Nov. 4. A drawdown can return reserves to banks, all else equal, while financing the government continues to place demands on cash and intermediaries.

Bitcoin’s price was about $77,865 in CryptoSlate’s market data at 10:41 UTC on Nov. 2, below $80,000. At the Nov. 2 morning check, Treasury’s release calendar still displayed August estimates and listed both November announcements as forthcoming.

The Fed’s Oct. 29 balance-sheet release put the Treasury General Account (TGA), the government’s operating account at the central bank, at $1,016 billion on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Treasury’s Aug. 3 borrowing forecast assumed an $850 billion cash balance at the end of December alongside $628 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing in the fourth quarter. Subtracting that old cash assumption from the October observation produces a gap of about $166 billion.

That comparison describes how far the account would have to fall to reach the August assumption.

A trillion-dollar account was also part of Treasury’s earlier planning. Its Aug. 5 refunding statement anticipated a late-October peak of $1.05 trillion, plus or minus $50 billion, citing the large outflows it expected around that time. That estimate described a cash buffer for upcoming payments. The Oct. 28 observation was inside that range, although a single observation cannot establish the eventual peak.

This makes the revised year-end assumption central. Retaining the old cash level would preserve a route to a substantial decline from the October observation. Raising the assumption would leave less room for that decline; lowering it would leave more.

The Nov. 2 release addresses the aggregate borrowing estimate and cash assumptions. The Nov. 4 refunding statement and schedules will add the instrument mix and buyback plans.

The reserve channel starts with payment accounting. As the Fed explains, Treasury payments move money from its account into a depository institution’s account at the central bank, either for the bank itself or for a customer. All else equal, that increases bank reserves.

Flows in the opposite direction absorb reserves through the same channel. Taxes paid into Treasury’s account and private purchases of government debt move funds toward the TGA. A projected cash drawdown therefore has to be understood alongside the financing and receipts that replenish the account. The realized net change in the account already reflects those incoming and outgoing cash flows.

The October data also show why Treasury cash cannot explain the entire reserve picture. Bank reserves averaged $2,894 billion in the week ended Oct. 28, down $69 billion from the previous weekly average. Over the same weekly-average comparison, the TGA rose $48 billion, other deposits increased $16 billion and total factors supplying reserves fell $1 billion.

These weekly averages describe a different measurement from the $1,016 billion Wednesday cash balance. Combining that point-in-time TGA figure with the weekly reserve change would blur the timing of the comparison.

Fed asset movements and shifts in other liabilities can also alter the result. A falling TGA would support reserves through one channel, but the realized reserve total and the behavior of short-term funding markets would determine whether conditions actually became easier.

Different types of borrowing place different demands on dealers and their clients. An Oct. 30 Fed staff study found that issuance increases dealer inventories and demand for client financing, with larger estimated balance-sheet effects from coupon securities, such as notes and bonds, than from bills.

Inventories generally unwind within several days, while financing demand can persist after the securities have moved to clients. The study’s main regression sample ran from January 2016 through June 2025.

Buybacks of outstanding Treasury debt can ease selected inventory burdens while the government continues to raise money. The department’s Aug. 19 announcement increased the maximum size of long-end liquidity-support operations from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation, effective Sept. 9 through Nov. 4. Treasury said it would provide more information about future sizes at the November refunding.

Those amounts are operation ceilings, not completed purchases. Treasury also says buybacks are not expected to significantly change privately held net marketable borrowing because new issuance replaces the securities bought back.

For Bitcoin, the relevant question is whether the combination leaves funding easier and investors more willing to carry risk. A lower cash assumption can coexist with issuance demands that keep intermediaries busy. The borrowing total, maturity composition and settlement schedule therefore need to be read together.

The proposed link to Bitcoin is a financial-conditions hypothesis. A 2023 IMF working paper found that Fed tightening reduced a broad crypto-price factor through investor risk-taking. Treasury cash management differs from a Fed policy change.

The useful test has several observable steps. A revised cash assumption would update the projected year-end balance. Subsequent balances would show whether the drawdown occurred. Stabilizing reserves and calmer repo funding, where securities are financed against collateral, would strengthen the case that the cash movement helped the wider funding backdrop.

For the demand side of that hypothesis, sustained net inflows into Bitcoin investment products and stronger spot buying alongside easier funding would be consistent with the relief thesis. Reserve relief without that demand would leave the price argument incomplete.

A higher cash target, continued reserve declines or persistent financing pressure would weaken the relief thesis. So would weak Bitcoin demand after funding conditions improved.

#5135. Texas brothers sentenced to 15 years for holding Minnesota family at gunpoint in $8 million crypto heist

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Raymond Christian Garcia and Isiah Angelo Garcia were sentenced to 15 years and 15.5 years, respectively for their roles in that September 2025 armed robbery.

Two brothers who held a family for nine hours at gunpoint in Minnesota for $8 million worth of cryptocurrency were sentenced to about 15 years in prison each, on Friday.

Two Texas men, Raymond Christian Garcia and Isiah Angelo Garcia, were sentenced to 15 years and 15.5 years, respectively, for their roles in that September 2025 armed robbery, according to a statement released by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota.

This comes after both brothers pleaded guilty to one count of interference with commerce by robbery back in June. In September 2025, Isiah Garcia pressed one of the victims, the father, to log into his crypto accounts and transfer funds to a crypto wallet that his brother then provided. However, the brothers later realized that the father had more crypto funds at a "hard drive-style cryptocurrency wallet" at a cabin three hours away, prosecutors said previously.

Later, the victim's son called 911, and the brothers fled, but were later tracked down by a Wendy's receipt, video surveillance of Raymond Garcia renting a motel room in Roseville, Minnesota, and a rental car, which led police to the brothers' house in Waller, Texas.

FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson said the brothers' actions were targeted and "extremely violent."

"Raymond and Isiah Garcia violated the sanctity of a home, abducted a victim, terrorized a family at gunpoint for hours, and disrupted an entire community in a brazen act of violence and greed," Dotson said in a statement on Friday.

#5134. Chrome Can Now Pull Details From Your Gmail to Fill Out Web Forms

Chrome Can Now Pull Details From Your Gmail to Fill Out Web Forms

Google’s Chrome browser can now pull personal details from your Gmail inbox to fill out online forms for you, the company said in its announcement on Wednesday.

The update, called “enhanced autofill,” suggests order numbers, tracking information, and flight bookings when a form asks for them, wrote Amanda Lim, a Chrome product manager, in the announcement. Autofill is the browser tool that types in details like your name and address so you don’t have to.

It runs on Gemini, Google’s AI assistant, through a feature called Personal Intelligence, which lets Gemini draw on connected apps such as Gmail and Google Photos to tailor its answers to your own life. It is rolling out to Gemini in Chrome users who have Personal Intelligence turned on, on desktop, Android and iOS, starting in the U.S.

Google’s post names only those three kinds of data as coming from Gmail. Credit card numbers and addresses are part of Chrome’s standard autofill, which fills them from details you have saved in the browser, and the announcement does not say the new feature pulls them out of your inbox.

“You can manage whether enhanced autofill is enabled and what it can access via your Chrome settings,” Lim wrote. “As always, sensitive data is encrypted and you remain in control.”

Encryption scrambles data so only Google and other authorized parties can read it, though the post does not explain how that applies to the Gmail content Chrome reads or what it scans.

Users choose whether to connect their apps and can switch the connections off at any time, the post says, though Google does train on limited information, such as specific prompts and the model’s responses.

In November, users pushed back on a Smart Features setting that let Gemini analyze emails and calendars unless they opted out, and Google said it had not changed its underlying data-handling practices.

Chrome also dropped a line from its settings saying on-device AI, meaning models that run on your own computer rather than Google’s servers, works without sending data to Google servers. Google said the wording change did not reflect a change in how it handles on-device AI.

The rollout began Wednesday in the U.S. on desktop, Android and iOS, and Google’s announcement gives no date for other countries

#5132. Arthur Hayes wants to hedge AI compute bills, but FLOP token swings could change the cost

His proposed dollar-settled contracts track a FLOP-priced benchmark, leaving inference buyers to match token, model and rollover exposure.

Arthur Hayes’s proposed AI-compute futures could offset a rise in a FLOP-priced benchmark while leaving a dollar-funded buyer exposed to the token’s exchange rate. The distinction affects businesses that would buy FLOP as they pay for inference, the work of running AI models to generate answers.

His October 26 blueprint connects financial contracts to FLOP Network, where AI agents would pay for model responses with the planned FLOP token. Receiving dollars from a hedge would stabilize the buyer’s dollar bill only to the extent that the contract matches its workload and currency exposure.

Hayes explicitly recognizes the currency link. He says pricing these proposed quanto contracts requires an adjustment for covariance between the compute index and the FLOP-dollar exchange rate, meaning how the two move together. Pricing that relationship and matching a particular customer’s bill are separate tasks: model choice, currency funding and purchase timing can leave residual exposure.

The market remains proposed. FLOP’s GPU-provider guide, updated October 30, says it operates only as a development network and involves no real money. Its official status page says no real FLOP token is trading.

Hayes calls the underlying index the Flop Reference Compute Rate, or FRCR. His essay labels it an hourly volume-weighted FLOP/GigaFLOPS rate and outlines quarterly futures and perpetual swaps that entrepreneurs could bring to traditional-finance or crypto exchanges.

The proposed quarterly contract uses USD margin and a multiplier of $1 per index point. A buyer going long one contract at 100 points would earn $100 if it settled at 200, before costs. That payment follows the change in the numerical index.

For a buyer acquiring tokens as it consumes inference, the bill has an additional conversion. It needs enough FLOP to purchase the workload and pays the dollar cost of acquiring those tokens. Even if the workload’s FLOP price follows FRCR exactly, the dollar bill also depends on the exchange rate at purchase.

The proposal also needs a settled measurement convention. FLOP tokens are currency; floating-point operations measure work; operations per second measure throughput. Hayes’s printed expression dividing a fee by work and then by latency does not dimensionally match a price per unit of throughput. The examples below therefore use numerical index points and an assumed workload relationship, rather than treating that expression as a verified conversion into physical compute.

Hypothetical starting bill: $100,000 at index 100 and $1/FLOP. The FLOP bill tracks the index; 1,000 long contracts use a fixed $1-per-point multiplier.

Index 200; token stays at $1. A $100,000 gain offsets the assumed bill increase.

Index stays at 100; token rises to $2. The $200,000 bill has no futures offset.

Index 200; token falls to $0.50. The bill is $100,000 and the gain is $100,000 before costs.

A matched index hedge alone does not fix dollar inference spending when the token exchange rate moves.

Hypothetical inputs and workload linkage, not FCUs, GPU-hours, quotes, forecasts or current USD-anchored bootstrap pricing. Excludes fees, margin timing, covariance-adjusted entry pricing, changing model/quantity, roll costs and default. Zero net in one case is not free compute or an available trade.

Illustrative fixed workload: FLOP bill=1,000×index; USD bill=FLOP bill×USD/FLOP. Long 1,000 contracts at index 100; gain=1,000×$1×(final index−100). Starting index100 and $1/FLOP give a $100,000 bill. Net=bill−gain. Exact arithmetic, no rounding.

Hypothetical inputs and workload linkage, not FCUs, GPU-hours, quotes, forecasts or current USD-anchored bootstrap pricing. Excludes fees, margin timing, covariance-adjusted entry pricing, changing model/quantity, roll costs and default. Zero net in one case is not free compute or an available trade.

Consider a hypothetical buyer whose fixed workload costs 100,000 FLOP when the index is 100. Assume its FLOP bill moves in direct proportion to that index. At an invented exchange rate of $1 per FLOP, the starting dollar bill is $100,000.

Give the buyer 1,000 long futures contracts entered at 100 points, each with Hayes’s proposed $1-per-point multiplier. For this example, that position offsets a proportional increase in the workload’s FLOP price when the token exchange rate stays at $1.

These scenarios let the numerical index and the FLOP-dollar exchange rate move independently for a buyer acquiring tokens as it consumes inference. A maintained dollar anchor could change that relationship, while prepaid forward purchases set token-acquisition costs upfront.

In the first case, the futures gain returns the net outlay to the original $100,000. In the second, the dollar bill doubles without an index move, so the futures pay nothing. In the third, the token’s fall already offsets the higher FLOP-denominated workload price, while the index-linked futures still produce a gain.

The zero is the bill minus that hypothetical gain, before fees, margin cash needs, covariance-adjusted entry pricing, model mismatch, roll costs or default.

FLOP’s present bootstrap pricing has a separate constraint. Its architecture FAQ describes inference prices in FLOP anchored to dollars. A maintained anchor can cause FLOP-denominated prices to adjust as the token exchange rate changes.

Currency is only one matching problem. Hayes’s reference rate is a composite, while the forward compute claims used to reproduce it are tied to particular models.

He acknowledges that a trader seeking synthetic FRCR exposure would need model-specific FLOP Compute Units, or FCUs, in the weights matching the index. Changes in the model mix alter that basket. A buyer using one model could therefore face a different price movement from the composite, even before converting FLOP into dollars.

The draft yellow paper defines an FCU as a specified amount of reference work under an identified metering profile and a supported model whose identity is fixed. That convention measures the work in the claim; a GPU’s advertised peak speed measures a different quantity.

Hayes illustrates longer exposure by rolling successive 30-day FCUs and describes perpetual exposure through continuous rolls. That approach depends on being able to replace positions at the required times and prices.

There is also a difference between his blueprint and the current draft specification. Hayes describes up to thirty daily FCU series for each model. The yellow paper instead specifies new standardized primary delivery starts from the next calendar day through fourteen days ahead, with seven days ahead as the default. Booking lead time is separate from the duration of delivery.

The current booking rules therefore qualify how the 30-day rolling example could be implemented. Standardized activation also remains gated on a completed executable profile, calibrated economics and a qualified physical pilot. The implementation matrix describes the FCU path as partial.

Collateral adds another dependency. Hayes’s forward design calls for fully funded purchase offers and provider bonds in FLOP. Backup providers and refunds address missed delivery, but his own description allows for circumstances in which replacement compute cannot be obtained. Receiving tokens back is a different outcome from receiving inference when it is needed.

Currency timing also depends on funding. If a buyer fully prepaid a specified forward claim using FLOP acquired at reservation, the dollar cost of acquiring those tokens would be incurred upfront. That would set the token-acquisition outlay for that purchase, while leaving delivery performance and other costs to be assessed.

The miner manual describes development inference and calibration, but says the SOFT verification tier’s full settlement and dispute path remains open and the HARD-tier bridge is not deployable.

As of November 2, FLOP’s testnet network page still labels the network planned and its release unreleased. The official timetable gives provisional targets of November 3 for testnet and Q1 2027 for mainnet and token generation.

The wider policy work is also exploratory. The CFTC’s August 19 consultation asked about compute cash-market liquidity, manipulation, customer protection and perpetual futures.

Hayes’s blueprint offers a way to transfer exposure to a compute index. For a buyer funding inference as it goes, predictable dollar spending would require the right combination of model-price and currency protection; his proposed rolling replication would also need executable forward rolls. A dollar settlement currency defines the contract’s payment, while the buyer’s purchasing arrangements determine how closely it protects the bill.

#5130. President Trump says they’re looking into Binance hack as calls grow for crypto rules

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

On Friday, The Digital Chamber CEO Cody Carbone sent a letter to House and Senate leadership, demanding that Congress immediately pass a bill that would give the CFTC authority over crypto exchanges.

Following the $6.3 billion hack of the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, calls are growing for legislation and for firms like Binance to move onshore.

On Thursday, Binance suffered that blow following what its co-CEO Richard Teng said was caused in part by a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop that gave an attacker access to a service container used to submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Blockchain analytics firms like TRM Labs have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a hacking unit in North Korea.

During a press conference on Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was looking into the hack, adding that Binance has said they are ensuring customers get their funds back.

"But it's a hack," he said. "That's the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check… these are different people, never see the money anymore. So I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous."

Earlier on CNBC, Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig pointed to Binance not being federally regulated by his agency as an issue. On Oct. 5, the agency proposed its federal framework for crypto, specifically for leveraged and margined retail crypto trading and a new registration category for exchanges offering those products.

"This proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Selig said. "The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States."

Both Republicans and Democrats have expressed concerns about Binance over the past few years, particularly when it came to money laundering and its consumer protections. In 2023, the exchange's previous CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls at Binance as part of a sweeping $4 billion settlement. He was later pardoned by Trump.

Whether or not the Clarity Act, broad crypto legislation to regulate exchanges along with other facets of the industry, would have helped freeze the transactions lost in the Binance hack also came up. The bill was passed by the House last year, but has since stalled in the Senate amid concerns over Trump's vast crypto wealth. That wealth had grown to hundreds of millions of dollars linked to World Liberty Financial and his TRUMP memecoin and became something many Democrats could not ignore in trying to pass the bill.

"Yesterday, hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance in less than 4 hours, the biggest heist in history," said one of the bill's negotiators, Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., in a post on X. "The Clarity Act would have given crypto firms legal cover to freeze suspicious transactions the instant law enforcement calls. Every minute lost is money gone for good."

Amanda Fischer, policy director and chief operating officer for Better Markets and who was the previous chief of staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission, pushed back, saying that the bill would have required stablecoin issuers to "freeze per a court order," adding that at the same time crypto firms worked as quickly as they could to freeze the assets, in a post on X.

However, Solana Policy Institute General Counsel Patrick Wilson said that wasn't right and that a section in the Clarity Act "expressly protected stablecoin issuers from private lawsuits for voluntary, temporary holds based on a reasonable belief of a violation of law. No court order required."

On Friday, The Digital Chamber CEO Cody Carbone sent a letter to House and Senate leadership, demanding that Congress immediately pass a bill that would give the CFTC authority over crypto exchanges and keep customer funds and company funds separate from each other in bankruptcy proceedings.

"No federal regulator can set and enforce consistent standards for how these platforms hold, segregate, and secure customer assets, or for their cybersecurity, before consumers are harmed," Carbone said. "Regulators can only act after the damage is done."

"We urge you to act before this Congress adjourns," he added.

Rep. Tom Timmons, R-S.C., meanwhile, brought up national security concerns.

"America cannot allow rogue regimes to exploit digital assets to finance their nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs," Timmons said in a post on X.

#5129. Coinbase Swings to $719 Million Q3 Profit on Crypto Gains

Coinbase Swings to $719 Million Q3 Profit on Crypto Gains

Coinbase is back in the black, though much of that came from the crypto on its own balance sheet.

The exchange reported third-quarter net income of $719 million, or $2.51 per diluted share, on Thursday, ending a two-quarter losing streak. Analysts had expected a loss of 15 cents per share, according to Zacks. But about $715 million of the profit came from gains on crypto Coinbase holds as an investment. Excluding those and other investment gains, adjusted net income was $78 million.

Total revenue came in at $1.22 billion, in line with expectations, flat from the second quarter and down 35% from a year earlier. Transaction revenue slipped 1% to $590 million but beat the roughly $527 million analysts expected, as crypto volatility sank to multiyear lows and trading volume across the market fell.

The standout was prediction markets, which crossed $200 million in annualized revenue, making it one of the fastest-growing products in Coinbase’s history, the company said.

Daily traders grew more than 60% from the prior quarter, and revenue has compounded 82% per quarter since launch. CEO Brian Armstrong said the product kept “growing even through slower sports months.”

“Prediction markets are adding another revenue stream and are less correlated to crypto volatility,” CFO Alesia Haas said.

Coinbase also cut its 2026 adjusted expense guidance by another $100 million at the midpoint, to between $4.15 billion and $4.3 billion, following cost reductions in May. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 60% from the prior quarter to $333 million. Through Oct. 25, fourth-quarter transaction revenue stood at about $165 million.

The positive results follow two consecutive losing quarters. Coinbase posted a $394 million loss in the first quarter and missed estimates in the second as trading activity slowed, though analysts said at the time they weren’t worried about the stock’s slide.

Shares closed Thursday at $160.59, down 1.1%, before the results came out, and were little changed in after-hours trading. The stock is down more than 55% from its 52-week high of $361.40.

#5128. Vitalik is making private Ethereum payments without a crypto website

Retaining local code can reduce repeated website delivery while leaving package updates, signatures and submission as separate trust decisions.

His objection goes beyond screen clutter. A website can deliver application code again whenever someone returns, leaving the user dependent on what the server supplies each time. Keeping a local application can reduce that repeated delivery exposure. It also moves a consequential decision onto the user: which software revision to install, retain and eventually replace.

The wallet he linked makes the trade-off concrete. Its documentation warns that the CLI is unaudited, under active development and written with AI assistance. It tells users to avoid mainnet unless they understand what they are doing and the possibility of catastrophic fund loss.

Control over a downloaded interface matters because the accepted code sits between a payment instruction and the signature authorizing it. Choosing when that code changes can reduce one recurring exposure, while its dependencies and signing access determine what the installed software can do.

The practical gain is the ability to keep a chosen application revision rather than obtaining the website interface again on each visit. Accepting a replacement revision creates another delivery decision. For this source-build route, that decision also involves the dependency set and the tools that turn source into executable software. A familiar project name alone does not describe all the code being accepted.

The documented installation route also shows what “local” entails. The project's instructions call for installing dependencies with npm install, building the application with npm run build, and running a local launcher. At commit 0ef5c44, the documentation, manifest, lockfile and implementation describe the same application revision. Its manifest identifies version 0.1.0 and requires Node.js 22 or later. Buterin's account does not identify his installed revision.

The manifest fixes direct dependency versions, including viem and several Kohaku packages. It also pins a separate kohaku-artifacts Git dependency to a commit. The corresponding lockfile records resolved registry packages and integrity hashes. The application therefore has a software supply chain even when its interface runs on the user's machine.

Kohaku-cli's public-transfer and Railgun unshield paths show why a pause before submission can mean different things. An ordinary public-transfer dry run returns without sending the transaction; a prepared Railgun unshield can already contain a signature.

For an ordinary, non-batched public transfer, the transfer implementation simulates the transaction and returns dry-run output without submission. The broadcast path requires the sender's private key, constructs a local wallet client and sends the transaction. The wallet-client code derives its signing account from that private key.

Private operations expose an additional wrinkle. The unshield command can output a prepared Railgun UserOperation that is already signed, even when broadcasting is withheld. A UserOperation is an account-operation payload that compatible tooling can submit. The separate broadcast implementation expects a signed operation and then sends it through a Pimlico bundler.

For that path, withholding submission can still leave a signed operation ready for compatible tooling to submit later. Calling the result “prepared” therefore does not make it universally unsigned. Software that may construct an authorization, software that may sign it and software that may submit it need to be assessed as distinct sources of authority, even when one CLI coordinates them.

Human confirmation is another separate choice. In the inspected public-transfer path, a suitably configured caller with wallet access can use --non-interactive together with --broadcast to submit without a further confirmation prompt. Wallet unlocking, required parameters, chain matching and simulation checks still apply. The capability is relevant to scripts and agents; it does not reveal whether Buterin uses unattended payments.

The README describes an encrypted seed on disk and owner-restricted password files for POSIX automation. Those measures govern stored secrets and how a process obtains access to them. They do not, by themselves, establish an independent spending limit or recipient policy once the process can use the signer.

CryptoSlate has previously covered the wallet-permission problem for local AI. Delivery control adds another dimension: a user can retain a chosen interface revision, while that code operates within whatever signing and submission authority it receives.

Software provenance offers a way to examine the delivery side more rigorously. It records where an artifact came from and how it was built. The SLSA verification standard describes checking a provenance signature, matching the artifact's digest, recognizing a trusted builder and comparing the stated source and build parameters with expected values.

These checks can help distinguish an expected build from a substituted artifact or an unintended build source. They still depend on which builders and source expectations the verifier trusts.

Dependency checking remains its own task. SLSA describes recursive verification of resolved dependencies as an optional additional step. Authenticating the top-level artifact does not automatically authenticate every input to it.

Correct origin and build history can accompany application logic that the user would still reject.

Buterin's experiment points to a concrete form of user control: choosing the application code that stays on the machine and deciding when to accept replacement code. Its value depends on carrying that control through dependency selection and the signer.

#5126. Inside the largest crypto hack on record: How attackers breached Binance for $6.3 billion

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Onchain investigators suggest the attackers exploited Binance's internal systems and wallet-signing mechanisms to move funds across multiple blockchains.

Binance was hit Thursday by the largest crypto hack to date, with blockchain investigators estimating that more than $6 billion in assets were stolen. Beyond the financial toll, the breach has raised questions about the security of centralized exchange infrastructure, particularly the hot wallets used to custody billions of dollars in customer assets.

Binance said its initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop and unauthorized access to a service container. The exchange has not identified a private-key leak, while co-CEO Richard Teng has described the attack as more complex than a compromise of a single employee's permissions.

Blockchain investigators have attributed the attack to North Korean hackers. Their analysis suggests the attackers exploited Binance's internal systems and wallet-signing mechanisms to move funds across multiple blockchains.

The attacker began staging at least 36 hours before the theft, funding an operational wallet with small Tornado Cash withdrawals, according to TRM Labs. It deployed and tested malicious code on three wallets before executing the attack.

On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper controlled by the attacker. It prepared 50 pre-signed authorizations to ensure one would remain valid when executed. TRM said coordinated transfers across nine other blockchains suggest a compromise of Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure.

Elliptic's analysis suggests the attacker retained access beyond the initial exploit, using one compromised wallet's owner rights to withdraw funds from another Binance wallet and repeatedly sweep new deposits. A second Ethereum hot wallet also sent $174 million in assets directly to the attacker, further pointing to access to Binance's broader transaction-signing infrastructure.

Simone Imbrescia, vice president of Immunefi, said the exploit highlights how an attack's sophistication does not necessarily lie in its onchain code, but in gaining access to the infrastructure capable of authorizing transactions.

"One of the striking things about this breach is how little code was actually needed on-chain. The sweeper contract was only around 130 lines," Imbrescia said. "The hard part sometimes is getting access to a system powerful enough to make very simple code devastating."

Chainalysis, Elliptic, and TRM attributed the attack to North Korean hacking groups, with TRM explicitly linking it to the same group connected to the $1.5 billion Bybit hack.

Chainalysis identified onchain links between funds stolen from Binance and proceeds from last month's Bitget exploit, which was also attributed to North Korean hackers. TRM cited similarities to previous North Korean operations, including Tornado Cash funding, advance staging and pre-signed authorizations. Elliptic also cautioned that the onchain overlap with the Bitget incident involved only a small portion of the Binance funds and did not conclusively establish that the same attackers were responsible.

Chainalysis identified thousands of transactions in a short period, with stolen funds repeatedly circulating between addresses. The attacker also attempted to avoid stablecoin freezes by converting $325 million in stablecoins into $285 million in ETH over nearly 20 minutes.

Elliptic said the attacker deposited $59.9 million in stolen USDT into Aave as collateral and borrowed 19,762 ETH. The loan remained open and was close to liquidation as of the firm's latest update. The attacker also swapped hundreds of millions of dollars in USDT for ETH through decentralized exchanges and market makers, accepting losses of as much as 26% against market prices to move funds into assets that issuers cannot freeze.

Aave said Friday that it had unfrozen all markets across its V3 and V4 protocols, adding that its smart contracts were unaffected and user positions remained fully collateralized.

Binance has approximately $5 billion in affected assets, with another $1.3 billion being acquired through market and OTC channels as part of its commitment to cover the losses.

Teng said the exchange was targeting Monday to publish its initial proof-of-reserves report and was working to restore withdrawals.

"We are very hopeful that users will be able to withdraw prior to our Sunday deadline, which is on track to be within 40 hours," Teng said in an X video on Friday.

TD Cowen analysts said the breach highlights the custody and cybersecurity risks associated with centralized exchanges but does not necessarily undermine the broader digital asset industry.

"The evidence available so far points to a compromise of infrastructure at a centralized intermediary, rather than a failure of Bitcoin or its underlying network," the analysts wrote. "Put differently, we do not stop using dollars when a bank is robbed, just as car theft does not invalidate the automobile."

The incident also highlights the need to secure the systems and processes that control access to private keys, Imbrescia said. Crypto security efforts often focus on protecting keys and auditing smart contracts, but the people, infrastructure and workflows capable of instructing those keys are part of the security perimeter, she added.

"If an attacker compromises that operational layer, they may not need to steal a key or discover an exotic smart-contract vulnerability at all," she said. "The broader lesson is that access controls, internal infrastructure and transaction-authorisation processes need to be secured with the same intensity as the keys themselves."

#5124. Strategy’s deployable cash falls 45% as buybacks outpace Bitcoin purchases

Strategy bought 811 BTC for $66 million and spent $208 million on STRC buybacks, while a separate $4.79 billion reserve backed dividend and debt-interest payments.

Strategy‘s deployable USD Cash fell 45.3% during the week ended Nov. 1, from $242 million to $133 million, as preferred-stock buybacks exceeded its Bitcoin purchases.

That balance is available for broader treasury uses. Strategy also held a separate $4.79 billion USD Reserve intended for preferred-stock dividends and debt interest.

The company bought 811 Bitcoin between Oct. 26 and Nov. 1 while setting another record for STRC preferred-stock buybacks.

The company spent approximately $66 million acquiring the cryptocurrency at an average price of $80,846 between Oct. 26 and Nov. 1, according to its Nov. 2 regulatory filing.

The purchase increased Strategy's holdings to 849,327 BTC, acquired for an aggregate $64 billion at an average price of $75,451 per coin.

The acquisition marked a return to larger Bitcoin purchases after Michael Saylor's firm suspended buying for a week while concentrating its spending on preferred-stock repurchases.

Strategy had acquired just 334 BTC, 250 BTC and 267 BTC in the first three reporting weeks of October, respectively. Its latest purchase was the largest since Sept. 28, when the company disclosed acquiring 1,665 BTC for approximately $143 million.

Strategy sold approximately 1,178,552 shares of its MSTR common stock through its at-the-market offering program, generating $164 million in net proceeds.

However, only $66 million, or about 40%, went toward purchasing Bitcoin. The remaining $99 million was allocated to the company's deployable USD Cash balance, which has come under pressure from its increasingly aggressive preferred-stock repurchase program.

The company did not issue any new preferred shares during the reporting period, leaving common-stock sales as its only source of fresh equity capital.

While Strategy resumed accumulating Bitcoin, its spending on STRC continued to accelerate.

The company repurchased approximately 2,092,035 STRC shares for $208 million, surpassing the previous weekly record of $205 million established in late October.

The latest transaction means Strategy spent more than three times as much repurchasing preferred shares as it did acquiring Bitcoin.

It also paid an average of approximately $99.52 per STRC share, bringing the transaction price within 0.5% of the security's $100 stated value. That compares with an average purchase price of approximately $99.06 the previous week.

STRC is a variable-rate perpetual preferred security carrying a 12% annualized dividend rate. Strategy has been purchasing the shares to support their trading price near $100 while reducing the amount of preferred capital outstanding.

Strategy entered the reporting period with approximately $242 million in USD Cash. Despite allocating another $99 million from common-stock sales to that balance, it finished the week with just $133 million after spending $208 million on STRC repurchases.

That represents a $110 million, or 45.3%, weekly decline in deployable cash.

The separate USD Reserve declined from approximately $4.83 billion to $4.79 billion after the company used $43 million to pay preferred-stock dividends during the reporting week. The reserve remains substantially larger than its flexible cash balance but serves a different purpose under the company's capital management framework.

Strategy has spent more than $2 billion on preferred-stock repurchases since it launched the program in July.

The company has about $749 million in remaining authorization under its expanded $3 billion digital credit securities repurchase program, along with an unused $1 billion authorization to repurchase MSTR common shares.

#5122. Binance Drained of $5.5 Billion in Suspected Hack, Tether and Circle Freeze $1.8 Billion

Binance Drained of $5.5 Billion in Suspected Hack, Tether and Circle Freeze $1.8 Billion

At least $5.57 billion in crypto has left wallets linked to Binance across three blockchains in what appears to be a breach of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.

If confirmed as a hack, it would be the biggest crypto hack on record. Binance has not confirmed its exchange has been hacked but said it is aware of the “potential security issue and is actively investigating.”

“We have not confirmed any impact to user funds,” the company posted on X. “Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information.”

Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. At this stage, we have not confirmed any impact to user funds.

Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official… pic.twitter.com/dN76yhzYM0

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange, where millions of people buy, sell and store their coins. The money came from its hot wallets, the internet-connected wallets exchanges use to process customer withdrawals.

The tally counts $3.51 billion on Ethereum, $1.44 billion in 18,270 Bitcoin and $630 million on Tron. The first Ethereum transaction, at 20:24 UTC, sent 167,464 ETH plus 63 token transfers to a brand-new address, including 1.615 billion USDT, a stablecoin built to always trade at $1, according to Etherscan.

Three minutes earlier, an address funded through Tornado Cash, a mixer that scrambles the trail of crypto payments, submitted a delegation for a Binance hot wallet using EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that lets an ordinary wallet run smart-contract code. “7702 lets a normal wallet execute delegated code. The delegation persists; that code can authorize later transfers without another signature from the wallet,” Odysseas Lamtzidi, founder of Phylax Systems wrote on X.

1/4 EIP-7702 can turn the wallet itself into the sweeper.

A Binance-labeled wallet moved 167,464 ETH + 63 tokens, including 1.615B USDT, just 3m24s after a signed delegation was installed.

This is bad.https://t.co/GrvUiya16D pic.twitter.com/zONu8cwW63

— Odysseus | phylax.systems (@odysseas_eth) October 29, 2026

How the attacker got the required signature is still unknown. Tether froze 975.1 million USDT in the main receiving address, and Circle, issuer of the rival stablecoin USDC, froze 823 million USDC in the same wallet at 21:04 UTC, bringing the total frozen to about $1.8 billion. Both issuers can block specific addresses from moving their tokens, but the attacker is moving funds fast.

"Circle is closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance," Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire posted on X. "In coordination with law enforcement, we have frozen more than 800M USDC associated with the incident and will continue supporting the investigation."

Total on the hack is at least $5.57B across 3 chains (likely more)

Tether has started freezing and this time even Circle acted and managed to freeze 800M in a single wallet.

Still $800M could be frozen, attacker is moving funds fast https://t.co/km4eyJWEa8 pic.twitter.com/IL6wBfZK2r

Binance lost 7,000 Bitcoin, about $40 million, in a 2019 hack. The $5.57 billion tally would be more than triple the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit heist in February 2025, the previous record.

#5120. Chainalysis says hacker using ‘offensive agentic techniques’ accessed its customers’ names and emails

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

In the midst of tracking the fallout from the multibillion-dollar Binance exploit, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed that its own customer data was accessed by an AI-assisted hacker.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said an unidentified hacker using "offensive agentic techniques" broke into its systems and internal tools this month and accessed some "non-sensitive" customer data, according to a notice sent to affected customers.

Chainalysis published the full text of the notice in a blog post on Friday evening. The attacker accessed "some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform," the company said, pledging to send a follow-up to each client detailing which exact information was accessed.

"Based on the evidence available to date, we have found no indication that these incidents resulted in the unauthorized access of investigation content (such as graphs, notes, or cases), transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, MFA secrets, or user session tokens," Chainalysis wrote.

Chainalysis did not say when it detected the intrusion, which was first flagged by International Cyber Digest, how many customers were affected, which specific vulnerabilities the attacker exploited, or how AI agents played a role in the breach. Chainalysis declined to answer specific follow-up questions from The Block.

Chainalysis said it has contracted third-party cybersecurity experts and is using large language models to support a broad security review of its platform. The firm advised affected firms to turn on two-factor authentication and to be on the lookout for suspicious activities like unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts.

Chainalysis said the incident is "not related to the recent crypto theft at Binance." Chainalysis, Elliptic and TRM have each attributed the roughly $6.3 billion Binance hack to North Korean hacking groups, which, according to Binance, managed to compromise an engineer's laptop and access a service container. The exchange's co-CEO Richard Teng said the breach was more complex than the compromise of a single employee's permissions, though.

On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper, The Block previously reported. The sweeper contract was only around 130 lines, Immunefi Vice President Simone Imbrescia said in a statement shared with The Block. "The hard part sometimes is getting access to a system powerful enough to make very simple code devastating," Imbrescia said.

Chainalysis, which puts the theft at $6.4 billion, has continued to track the stolen funds. On Friday, the firm said it was seeing "never-seen-before laundering patterns," with thousands of transactions in a short period suggesting the attackers were using automation to obscure the trail. Rather than simply forwarding funds to new addresses, the attackers repeatedly circulated the stolen crypto among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses used earlier in the sequence, the firm said, sharing a diagram showing the funds' movements.

On Saturday, Chainalysis said the exploiters have used DeFi lending protocols on the Tron network to stay ahead of stablecoin freezes since the early hours of the attack. The hackers swapped Tron's native TRX token for various stablecoins and deposited them in a lending protocol, identified by onchain analysts Specter and Ian Unsworth as JustLend, in exchange for receipt tokens, which cannot be frozen by stablecoin issuers. The attackers then moved those receipts to clean wallets, redeemed them for stablecoins and bridged the funds off Tron, swapping them for ETH on the other side, according to the firm.

"Now the exploiter is free of worry of a freeze," the firm wrote. Chainalysis' Saturday thread noted that around $2.8 billion in stablecoins have already been frozen by stablecoin firms such as Circle and Tether. "Of course, exchanging stablecoins for ETH does not make the hackers bulletproof," Chainalysis added.

#5119. Tether freezes $4.5 million as Mercado Bitcoin hacker holds $46 million in crypto

Security researchers identified $9.17 million in frozen assets as the Brazilian exchange became the latest target in a wave of attacks following Binance's record $6.3 billion hack.

Tether has frozen more than $4.5 million in USDT linked to a security breach at Brazilian crypto exchange Mercado Bitcoin.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino confirmed the freeze on Nov. 2, saying the stablecoin issuer blocked more than 4.5 million USDT linked to the incident.

Notably, Tether is a major investor in the exchange. The stablecoin issuer announced a $20 million strategic investment in Mercado Bitcoin in July to support its expansion into tokenization, payments, and other digital financial services.

Meanwhile, on-chain analyst Specter reported that coordinated efforts involving security researchers and stablecoin issuers had expanded the immobilized assets to more than $9 million across nine digital assets, including USDC, PAXG, RLUSD, and others.

The intervention came as blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence identified approximately $46 million in cryptocurrency held by wallets attributed to the attacker, including $8.37 million in Ethereum, $8.24 million in Bitcoin and $1.76 million in PEPE.

Earlier today, Mercado Bitcoin disclosed that it had identified and contained a security incident affecting one of its systems overnight.

The exchange temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating suspicious asset movements but maintained that customers suffered no financial losses and that no personal information was compromised.

However, it has not disclosed the financial extent of the attack or explained whether its corporate reserves were affected.

Mercado Bitcoin subsequently published suspicious destination addresses across Bitcoin, Ethereum-compatible networks, Solana, Stellar and Tron to support tracing and potential recovery efforts.

The Mercado Bitcoin breach comes less than four days after hackers stole a record $6.3 billion from Binance on Oct. 29, extending a series of major attacks against centralized crypto exchanges.

Binance's incident followed a $388 million security breach at Bitget on Sept. 24, when attackers siphoned assets from the exchange's wallet infrastructure. Bitget subsequently tapped its protection fund to absorb the losses and protect customer balances.

The attacks have revived concerns about the security of centralized trading platforms, which collectively custody billions of dollars in digital assets and depend on internal systems to authorize transfers.

A similar pattern emerged in 2025, when two major exchanges suffered substantial losses within weeks of each other.

In February, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion after hackers manipulated the transaction approval process for one of its Ethereum cold wallets. The incident followed a $69 million hot-wallet breach at Phemex in January.

Although the incidents involved different attack methods, they exposed vulnerabilities in wallet management, transaction authorization, and the infrastructure exchanges rely on to safeguard customer assets.

The North Korean-linked TraderTraitor operation has been implicated in the two largest attacks. The FBI attributed both the Bybit and Binance thefts to North Korean hackers, demonstrating how sophisticated threat actors have repeatedly targeted centralized custodians.

However, investigators have not established any connection between those operations and the latest Mercado Bitcoin breach.

#5118. Binance Hacker Hunts for Exit Ramps as DeFi Exchanges Pause Markets

Binance Hacker Hunts for Exit Ramps as DeFi Exchanges Pause Markets

The attacker behind the wallets draining Binance is using decentralized exchanges such as Uniswap and Aave as exits, swapping stablecoins that issuers can freeze for Ethereum that nobody can, according to Etherscan records for 10 wallets, eight of them labeled as exploiters.

Earlier today, wallets linked to the world’s largest crypto exchange were drained of at least $5.5 billion, with the total tally still climbing. The company said it was investigating the security incident but did not confirm user funds were affected, though security experts widely believe the exchange was indeed hacked. It stands to be the largest hack in the crypto industry's 18-year history.

Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle moved quickly to blacklist the suspected attacker’s addresses in order to freeze a portion of the funds and make them inaccessible. As centralized issuers, they each have the ability to blacklist addresses so their tokens cannot move, and more than $2 billion of those two tokens have been frozen so far by different stablecoin providers. ETH has no issuer, so every dollar converted before a freeze lands is out of their reach.

The swaps run through Uniswap, a decentralized exchange where trades settle automatically with no company in the middle.

One relay wallet received 20,940 ETH ($45.58 Million) from Uniswap’s UniswapX contract at 20:34 UTC, another got 3,552 ETH (over $8 million) at 20:47, and two later wallets took in about 18,085 ETH (around $41 million) from Uniswap contracts, in 7,444 ETH and 10,642 ETH batches, and about 16,498 ETH ($37.5 million), in 6,946 ETH and 9,552 ETH batches.

Aave, a lending app where users deposit crypto as collateral to borrow other coins, offered a second exit. Between 20:57 and 21:01 UTC, one wallet deposited $10 million and then $50 million in USDT and borrowed 3,271 ETH ($7.43 million) and then 16,491 ETH ($37.47 million) against it, which prompted cybersecurity experts Odysseas Lamtzidi, founder of Phylax Systems, to warn of “contagion in full effect.”

Contagion in full effect https://t.co/aNz2snt8E6

— Odysseus | phylax.systems (@odysseas_eth) October 29, 2026

Aave has since frozen its V3 markets on Ethereum mainnet, which blocks new deposits and borrowing.

Kamino, a decentralized finance protocol built on the Solana blockchain, also paused its Solana and Bitcoin markets as a precautionary measure.

Kamino can confirm that it is currently unaffected by the ongoing Binance situation

Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily paused borrowing in the SOL/BTC Market

We are actively monitoring the situation and are in communication with various partners. Any further…

The ETH is piling up rather than moving on. A wallet labeled Exploiter 8 still held 195,460 ETH ($444.2 million) at 22:03 UTC, and another 57,891.77 ETH ($131.6 million) reached one labeled Exploiter 11, together about 253,000 ETH, or roughly $570 million. That second pile arrived after four hops in 28 minutes, from Exploiter 4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 7 and 7 to 11.

The attacker also swapped 36 million RLUSD, Ripple’s dollar-backed stablecoin, for 15,439 ETH, while 52.54 million RLUSD remained unfrozen at the holding wallet, according to an on-chain update circulating on X. Etherscan showed the main receiving wallet holding about $88.5 million in RLUSD at 20:41 UTC, which matches the two figures combined.

Ripple has since frozen about $200 million, according to Binance co-CEO Yi He. “Thanks to the Ripple team for promptly freezing approximately 200 million. User Funds are SAFU,” a reference to the exchange’s emergency reserve fund, Yi He wrote on X.

“Ripple is closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and its attackers’ RLUSD holdings and we are actively freezing affected funds,” Jack McDonald, Ripple’s senior vice president for stablecoins, said in a statement. “We’re coordinating with relevant parties and stand ready to support any investigation and appropriate action to keep users protected.”

Ripple is closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and its attackers’ RLUSD holdings and we are actively freezing affected funds. We’re coordinating with relevant parties and stand ready to support any investigation and appropriate action to keep users…

— Jack McDonald (@_JackMcDonald_) October 29, 2026

Tornado Cash, a mixer that scrambles the trail of crypto payments, appears so far only as funding for the address that set up the attack.

#5116. Strategy (MSTR) Adds 811 Bitcoin, Strive (ASST) Follows Suit With 124 as Both Keep Stacking

Strategy bought 811 bitcoin for $65.5 million and Strive added 124 BTC last week, with the two firms together adding 935 coins and Strategy now holding 849,327 BTC.

Strategy bought another 811 bitcoin last week. The Saylor-led firm spent about $65.5 million at an average of $80,846 per coin between October 26 and November 1, according to its 8-K filing on Monday. That brings total holdings to 849,327 BTC, bought for roughly $64.1 billion at an average of $75,451.

The money didn’t come from new preferred stock this time. Strategy sold about 1.18 million shares of MSTR common stock for roughly $164 million, sent $65.5 million into bitcoin, and parked the remaining $98.5 million in USD cash. It also spent around $208 million buying back about 2.1 million shares of its STRC preferred.

Strategy spent much of the year leaning on preferred issuance to fund purchases, and the company is now using the buyback to tidy up its preferred stack while still adding coins.

Saylor teased the purchase Sunday with his usual tracker chart and a line that made the rounds on X: “We found room for even more orange.”

The buy landed a few days after Strategy reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Net income hit $19.5 billion, up from $2.79 billion a year earlier, driven by a $20.9 billion operating gain tied to the bitcoin price rising during the quarter. That gain is a paper one under fair-value accounting, not cash. Saylor called it the start of the next bitcoin bull market and pointed to bitcoin trading about 21% above its 200-week moving average. The same release said CFO Andrew Kang will step down November 5, with COO Reza Virasteh taking over the role in January.

Strategy shareholders also recently approved a proposal allowing four preferred stocks — STRF, STRC, STRK, and STRD — to accrue dividends daily, including weekends and holidays, with 99.3% of votes cast in favor. The change was intended to improve liquidity, reduce reinvestment delays, and increase price stability, while keeping dividend rates and total obligations unchanged. The new payment schedule remained subject to board approval and regulatory filings, with implementation expected to begin in November 2026 for STRC and January 2027 for the other preferred stocks.

BREAKING: Public companies Strive and Strategy bought a combined 934 Bitcoin worth $72.6 million.Strategy: 810 BTCStrive: 124 BTC pic.twitter.com/ObXGCz7weH

Strive is still in the race for second place among public holders. The Matt Cole-run firm added 124 BTC between October 24 and 30 at about $80,526 each, lifting its stack to 43,124 BTC.

That’s a smaller buy than its previous week, when it added more than 6,000 coins, but Cole has been consistent about his approach. He has said the company is buying “hand over fist” when prices dip, and he has framed the funding model around perpetual preferred equity as a way to avoid forced selling.

Strive’s cash position slipped about $14 million to $490 million over the same stretch, and it still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s STRC.

Meanwhile, the biggest story in crypto last week wasn’t a buy. On October 29, Binance was hit by what it now estimates is a $6.3 billion security breach, one that started with a compromised DevOps laptop.

Blockchain analytics firms including Chainalysis and TRM Labs have linked the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and the drain reportedly took about 20 minutes. Binance says it has frozen roughly $3 billion of the stolen funds and will cover losses from its SAFU fund and company reserves.

Bitcoin slid toward $76,000 on the news, and it fell about 3.6% over the week.

Strategy’s stock dropped about 9% last week and closed Friday at $130.51. The company still has about $18.6 billion of MSTR available under its ATM program, which means more buys are likely if the market cooperates.

Strive shares were down around 20% last week. At the time of writing, bitcoin is near $78,000.

#5115. Hackers hijack a dozen DeFi websites, all registered with Name.com, and steal about $138,000

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Blockaid said the sites were rigged with Step Drainer, a malware kit that tricks visitors into signing away their funds. Ten of the domains have since been suspended.

Hackers who took over a dozen DeFi websites late Friday and used them to empty visitors' crypto wallets targeted domains registered through the same company, Name.com, according to public registry records reviewed by The Block. The Block has traced about $138,000 in stolen funds so far using onchain data.

Name.com is listed as the registrar for all 12 hijacked sites that were identified by security firm Blockaid, and 10 of them were suspended at the registrar level at 8:32 a.m. ET on Saturday.

X user bluexxix was among the first to notice the shared registrar, posting at 11:51 p.m. ET on Friday that it "seems @namedotcom is compromised" as more affected sites surfaced. Pseudonymous developer banteg reached the same conclusion on Saturday morning, and X user punkquidity later spotted that 10 of the domains had been switched off within seconds of each other.

Each of the 10 suspended domains now carries a "client hold" status, which stops a domain from resolving. They include Pickle Finance, Origami Finance, FluxBeam, Echelon, StonkFun and StakePoint. Flap's and Kintsu's domains were not suspended and are still operational as of publishing time.

X user liquidated0x flagged that Flap's site had seemingly been compromised at 9:10 p.m. ET on Friday, about an hour before the token launchpad warned its users that its flap.sh frontend had been hit by "a DNS hijacking incident." Blockaid warned about the attack on Flap and liquid staking protocol Kintsu at 10:54 p.m. ET, naming the 10 additional hijacked sites soon after.

Name.com's only public response so far came at 12:27 a.m. ET, when it replied to liquidated0x and bluexxix on X, asking them to fill out its abuse form. Name.com’s listed press address did not accept The Block’s request for comment, and its parent company, Identity Digital, did not immediately respond.

Blockaid said the hijacked sites were rigged with Step Drainer, a malware toolkit that tricks visitors into approving transfers out of their wallets once they connect them to a site. Security firm LevelBlue SpiderLabs described Step Drainer in April as a "Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS)" kit, reportedly sold for about $750 for the full source code or $150 for a version that takes a 20% cut of each theft. The firm said the kit claims support for more than 20 blockchain networks.

Onchain data reviewed by The Block shows the attackers routing proceeds to three wallets in fixed 15%, 55% and 30% cuts. On BNB Chain, a Safe wallet flagged by liquidated0x received about 3.1 BNB, worth roughly $2,200, from four wallets between 9:00 and 9:42 p.m. ET on Friday. It split the first three deposits among the three wallets, and about 2.27 BNB was still sitting in the Safe on Saturday morning.

The same three wallets received identically split payments on Ethereum, Robinhood Chain, and Monad, the network Kintsu runs on. On Monad, two of the wallets redeemed Kintsu's staked MON token and withdrew from lending protocol Neverland before converting the proceeds into MON. On Robinhood Chain, one wallet pulled tokenized stocks including NVDA and AAPL out of Morpho and swapped them for ETH.

Together the three wallets held about $138,000 late Saturday morning, mostly MON and Robinhood Chain ETH, and almost all of it arrived after the attack started. That's only what The Block could trace on EVM chains. Three of the hijacked sites, FluxBeam, StonkFun and StakePoint, are built on Solana, and Echelon runs on Aptos, so any losses there would sit in other wallets and aren't counted.

The hijacked sites don't share a DNS provider, the service that tells internet browsers which server a domain points to. Some run on Cloudflare, some on Vercel and some on Name.com's own nameservers. Punkquidity said they couldn't yet tell "whether Name.com itself or a reseller like Vercel did it."

Kintsu and Origami Finance have both publicly blamed cloud infrastructure firm Vercel. "It was something that happened on Vercel's end that was out of our control," Kintsu wrote in a reply on X, adding that Vercel had not yet responded. Origami first warned of "an active attack on Vercel-associated Nameservers," and later said its vaults would stay paused while it waits for "root cause analysis from Vercel / name[.]com." Flap builder Cedric said shortly after midnight that the team was reaching out to both companies.

Vercel picked Name.com as the registrar for its rebuilt domain service last year, Name.com said in a December 2025 press release. Vercel had not commented publicly as of Saturday morning, and both companies' status pages listed all systems as operational. In April, Vercel disclosed a breach of its internal systems that it traced to a compromised third-party AI tool, The Block previously reported.

No affected project has reported a victim count as of yet, though onchain data shows at least four wallets sent funds to the attackers on BNB Chain alone. FluxBeam said it had "no reports of users being affected," and StonkFun, which moved its site to new infrastructure overnight, said it was "not aware of anyone affected." Kintsu, Origami, FluxBeam and StonkFun all said their onchain contracts were untouched.

Crypto front-ends have been hit by DNS hijacks before. Aerodrome and Velodrome were hijacked in November 2025, and Galxe was hit in October 2023, when attackers got into the project's account at registrar Dynadot.

Vercel did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Blockaid's PR agency said the firm was looking into The Block's questions.

The suspensions on the hijacked domains appear to have been lifted by late Saturday morning, registry records show. The domains resolve again and now carry locks that block transfers and, for most of them, other changes.

Name.com has allegedly told at least one affected project that the breach was not on its end. Cloakd, the developer behind FluxBeam, said on X that its representative at Name.com was "taking the stance that it’s not them but the 3rd party issuers."

Updated at 2:00 p.m. ET with details from the lifted suspension and Cloakd's post.

Update, Oct. 31, 3:37 p.m. ET: Name.com said 15 customer domains were affected, more than the 12 Blockaid identified.

"name.com identified unauthorized activity late Friday, October 30, that redirected a number of domains registered through the platform,” a Name.com spokesperson said in a statement to The Block. "name.com has restored all affected domains and is working directly with the name.com account holders. We’re continuing to investigate and have taken steps to secure the accounts involved."

Name.com also said on X that the domains "were improperly redirected late Friday as part of a plan to access visitors’ crypto wallets," and urged customers to check their DNS records and enable two-factor authentication. Vercel said in a security bulletin that 10 of the affected domains were associated with its platform, that Name.com has restored them and that it is assisting in the investigation.

#5114. Binance warns of second wave of crypto theft as $6.3 billion hack recovery continues

The exchange has completed reserve verification for 10 cryptocurrencies but says scammers could exploit customers seeking withdrawals and compensation.

Binance has warned customers about potential scams exploiting withdrawal delays as the exchange recovers from a $6.3 billion security breach.

In a Nov. 2 security advisory, the exchange said fraudsters could take advantage of its phased withdrawal reopening by impersonating Binance representatives and offering customers assistance with delayed transactions, compensation claims and asset recovery.

The warning covers fraudulent emails, direct messages, group chats and even small cryptocurrency transfers carrying malicious instructions.

According to Binance, scammers may promise to speed up pending withdrawals, sell customers priority access to withdrawal queues, or instruct them to transfer their holdings into supposedly secure wallets.

The exchange emphasized that it does not charge fees to unlock withdrawals, offer paid recovery services or ask customers to authorize wallet transactions to regain access to their funds.

It also warned against fraudulent proof-of-reserves websites and compensation eligibility links, which could become particularly deceptive as the exchange introduces new verification tools following the breach.

Once customers approve malicious wallet permissions, attackers can transfer their assets without further authorization, potentially creating losses that cannot be reversed.

The warning comes as Binance attempts to restore normal operations after an Oct. 29 attack that compromised its hot wallets and resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies.

Meanwhile, Binance announced on Nov. 2 that it had completed the zero-knowledge proof for its Oct. 31 reserve snapshot, allowing customers to independently verify the backing of ten major cryptocurrencies.

The covered assets include Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB, XRP, Solana, Zcash, and four stablecoins: USDT, USDC, USD1, and RLUSD.

Binance said the completed proof lets customers verify that their balances were included in the snapshot and backed by reserves of at least 1:1, without revealing individual account holdings.

The process requires users to obtain account-specific verification information and download a verification tool through Binance's official proof-of-reserves platform.

However, the verification applies to balances recorded at 00:00 UTC on Oct. 31 and does not establish the exchange's current financial position or independently audit its overall solvency.

The announcement also comes as Binance continues replenishing assets affected by the theft.

According to the exchange, approximately 95% of the impacted assets have been replaced using company resources, while the remaining 5% consists of less-liquid cryptocurrencies that are more difficult to acquire in sufficient quantities.

Binance has been sourcing those assets through market purchases and over-the-counter transactions, separately from efforts to trace and recover the original stolen funds.

The exchange began restoring withdrawals on Nov. 1, with access returning progressively across supported cryptocurrencies and blockchain networks.

Another phase is scheduled for Nov. 3, although Binance has yet to confirm which additional assets and networks will become available.

The prolonged reopening gives fraudsters an opportunity to exploit customers awaiting access to their funds, particularly through fake support channels and requests for wallet authorizations.

Binance has instructed customers with pending withdrawals to check their status directly through its application and verify suspicious communications using its official verification service.

The exchange plans to publish another reserve snapshot on Nov. 4 covering additional cryptocurrencies. Generating the accompanying zero-knowledge proof is expected to take another 40 to 50 hours.

#5111. Binance Finds 'Additional Points of Breach' in $6.3B Hack

Binance Finds 'Additional Points of Breach' in $6.3B Hack

Binance has uncovered "additional points of breach" in Thursday's security incident, which it estimates cost around $6.3 billion, the exchange said on Friday, after initially pointing to a compromised engineer's laptop.

In an announcement late Thursday, Binance said a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. "We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," the exchange said.

Investigation update: Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.

This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination… pic.twitter.com/FQQ3vKT6GU

Binance CEO Richard Teng said on Friday that the attacker "did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action," describing "a more complex attack process." "Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," he wrote.

"This was a complex attack," Binance said in its latest update, adding that it is still gathering the facts. Outflows stopped when it paused withdrawals, and it remains on track to resume them in 45 hours, the exchange said.

I want to speak to you directly about what happened.

Bottom line - your money is safe, and we're covering every loss.

Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. That gave an attacker access to a…

— Richard Teng (@_RichardTeng) October 30, 2026

About $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen onchain with the help of blockchain partners, Binance said. The exchange said it will cover all losses from its SAFU fund, an emergency reserve for users, and from company funds, and that "user funds are safe."

Binance initially suspended deposits and withdrawals, revoked the affected address authorization, and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the funds. By Friday morning, deposits were "operating as normal," Teng said, while withdrawals remain suspended as the exchange completes "a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses."

"We'll share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified—and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete," Teng wrote.

Blockchain analytics firm Arkham put the haul at $6.01 billion, taken from Binance hot wallets on nine blockchains between 4:10 p.m. and 7:05 p.m. ET on Thursday, it said in a tweet. Issuers had frozen $2.80 billion of it, but $2.9 billion in Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and other tokens could still be moved, according to Arkham.

The attacker has kept moving funds. Early Friday, the wallets sent $38.82 million in Ethereum to a new address, while still holding $1.12 billion in ETH, Arkham said. Hours later, a Tron address tagged by Arkham as belonging to the attacker sent about $2.1 million in TRX to nine new addresses in 14 transfers, according to Arkham data.

Stablecoin issuers moved quickly as the funds left Binance. Tether and Circle froze about 975.1 million USDT and 823 million USDC held in the main receiving wallet, worth about $1.8 billion, Decrypt reported on Thursday, when an onchain tally put the drain at $5.57 billion. Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao thanked the two issuers for their "quick freeze."

As of Friday morning, Arkham's entity page for the attacker showed holdings of about 18,270 BTC, 488,364 ETH, 663.6 million TRX and 970,551 SOL, alongside frozen stablecoin balances.
